The Proponents approach to ensuring project delivery is on time and within budget.
a) The onboarding process for new clients at CGI indeed includes several key components to ensure alignment of expectations and smooth integration. This process involves:

Alignment of Expectations: CGI emphasizes the importance of understanding the Client Partnership Management Framework (CPMF) to align both parties on culture and expectations. This includes discussions on project goals, communication protocols, and performance metrics.

Service Level Agreements (SLAs): Establishing clear SLAs is crucial for defining the expectations regarding service delivery, response times, and quality standards. These agreements help ensure that both CGI and the client have a mutual understanding of the service commitments.

Introduction of Team Members: New clients are introduced to their project team members, which fosters communication and collaboration. A list of project team contacts with roles is provided to facilitate lines of communication and issue resolution.

Detailed Procedures: CGI provides comprehensive training on operational procedures, including where to store documents, how to access systems, and the incident management process. This training is tailored to the specific needs of the client and includes a review of pertinent SLAs and the responsibilities of each team member.

Documentation and Resources: Clients receive onboarding packs that include essential documentation and resources, ensuring they have access to necessary information from the outset. This includes guidelines on using ticketing systems and understanding the incident management process.
Overall, the onboarding process is designed to be completed within 30 days or less, ensuring that new team members are fully integrated and ready to contribute effectively to the client's needs.
b) CGI ensures engagements are adequately resourced through a comprehensive and proactive resource management approach. Key elements of this approach include:

Cooperative Account Management: CGI assigns a senior management team member to each account, who collaborates closely with the client's leadership, business, and technical teams. This relationship helps CGI understand the client's needs and vision, allowing for better prediction of changes in resource requirements and the ability to scale teams up or down as necessary.

Proactive Planning: Ongoing communication with clients is maintained to ensure that CGI understands their resource needs. This proactive approach allows CGI to plan and have resources ready for deployment when required, minimizing delays and ensuring that the right expertise is available at the right time.

Dynamic Internal Resourcing: CGI can dynamically assign resources to project and operational teams based on the client's changing priorities. This flexibility is supported by a global pool of resources, enabling quick adjustments to meet project demands.

Weekly Resource Management Reviews: CGI's local management team conducts weekly reviews of resource utilization and upcoming project requirements. This regular assessment helps identify any potential resource shortages early and allows for timely adjustments to resource allocation.

Expertise Transfer and Recruitment: CGI has a strong capability to recruit, assign, and mobilize relevant resources, even in contexts of resource shortages. The company has demonstrated its ability to adjust to fluctuations in resource needs effectively, ensuring that clients receive the necessary expertise throughout the engagement.

Workforce Optimization Strategy: CGI implements strategies to identify workforce gaps, plan for transitions, and reduce the risk of long-term vacancies. This strategy aims to maximize the effectiveness of the project team and ensure continuity throughout the project lifecycle.

Overall, CGI's resource management processes are designed to provide clients with quick and effective access to the necessary resources, ensuring that engagements are adequately supported at all times.
c) CGI implements a robust framework to guarantee the quality of service delivered to clients. Key components of this quality assurance approach include:

Quality Management System: CGI employs a comprehensive quality management system known as the "CGI Management Foundation," which is aligned with ISO 9001 certification. This system is regularly evaluated through routine project monitoring, customer satisfaction evaluations, internal audits, and external audits to ensure compliance and continuous improvement.

Quality Assurance Framework: The Client Partnership Management Framework (CPMF) is utilized to ensure quality throughout all project phases, from proposal to contract completion. This framework helps in establishing clear quality expectations and monitoring adherence to these standards.

Structured Requirements Management: CGI has a documented process for defining, documenting, and managing requirements that affect service delivery. This structured approach ensures that all requirements are clearly specified, and any changes are carefully controlled and documented, minimizing the risk of miscommunication or oversight.

Development and Testing Processes: CGI follows industry standards and modern Agile practices in its development processes. This includes extensive testing and verification processes, such as unit testing, integration testing, and user acceptance testing, to ensure that the products and services meet the highest quality standards.

Continuous Improvement: CGI's proprietary Quality System is designed for continuous improvement, utilizing various methods and measures such as metrics, analysis, and reporting. This system enables CGI to provide quality assurance of processes and deliverables, ensuring that client expectations are consistently met.

Collaboration and Feedback: CGI emphasizes collaboration with clients and stakeholders throughout the project lifecycle. Regular feedback loops are established to assess service quality and make necessary adjustments, ensuring that the final deliverables align with client expectations.

ITIL Framework Alignment: CGI leverages the ITIL framework to enhance its quality management practices. This alignment ensures that best practices in service delivery are followed, and ongoing training is provided to CGI members to maintain high standards of service quality.
Overall, CGI's quality assurance mechanisms are designed to ensure that services and products delivered meet the highest standards, fostering client satisfaction and trust.
d) CGI emphasizes effective communication and management of expectations with stakeholders throughout the project lifecycle. Key aspects of this approach include:

Stakeholder Engagement Strategy: CGI develops a comprehensive stakeholder engagement and communication strategy that outlines how and when interactions will occur. This strategy is designed to manage stakeholder expectations and keep them engaged with the project.

Identification of Key Stakeholders: Within the first three months of engagement, CGI identifies all internal and external stakeholders. This identification process is crucial for understanding the needs and expectations of each stakeholder, allowing for tailored communication strategies.

Assessment of Needs and Expectations: CGI analyzes the needs and expectations of stakeholders to prioritize them effectively. This assessment helps in tailoring strategies that align with stakeholder interests and project goals.

Establishment of Communication Channels: CGI establishes clear communication channels, including proactive updates through newsletters and email communications. This ensures that stakeholders are kept informed about project progress and any changes that may impact them 2.

Feedback Mechanisms: The engagement plan incorporates feedback cycles customized to stakeholder priority. This allows for regular follow-ups on feedback outcomes, ensuring that stakeholder concerns are addressed promptly and effectively.

Transparent Communication: CGI ensures open and transparent communication with clients, providing regular updates on project progress, challenges, and changes. This transparency is vital for managing expectations and maintaining a positive project reputation.

Workshops and Co-Creation Sessions: CGI involves clients in workshops and co-creation sessions to collaboratively define needs and expectations. This participatory approach fosters a sense of ownership among stakeholders and enhances collaboration.

Overall, CGI's communication and management strategies are designed to foster strong relationships with stakeholders, ensuring that their needs are met and that they remain engaged throughout the project.

e) CGI's approach to risk management is comprehensive and structured, ensuring that potential risks are identified, assessed, and mitigated throughout the project lifecycle. Key elements of this approach include:

Early Identification of Risks: CGI emphasizes the importance of identifying risks as early as possible in the project lifecycle. This proactive approach allows for the development of mitigation strategies and supports sound management decisions.

Risk Management Plan: A detailed risk management plan is developed at the project's initiation phase. This plan outlines the initial list of risks, preliminary mitigation strategies, and the governance structure for ongoing risk management.

Risk Assessment and Analysis: CGI conducts thorough assessments of identified risks, considering their causes, potential consequences, and the probability of occurrence. Risks are quantitatively categorized and prioritized for monitoring, ensuring that the most critical risks receive appropriate attention.

Monitoring and Control: The project manager is responsible for monitoring risk responses through mechanisms such as a risk register or risk log. This ongoing monitoring helps detect changes in the risk environment and ensures that mitigation activities are effective.

Integration with Project Management: CGI's risk management approach is integrated with other project management processes, contributing to a continuous cycle of risk identification, analysis, and mitigation. This integration ensures that risk management is a fundamental aspect of project delivery.

Documentation and Reporting: Risks are documented, monitored, and reported on throughout the project. This includes defining roles and responsibilities for the project team in managing risks and establishing tools for tracking and reporting.

Issue Management: Unresolved risks are addressed through issue management processes, which involve identifying, logging, researching alternatives, and documenting recommendations for resolution. This structured approach ensures that issues are managed effectively.
Overall, CGI's risk management methodology is designed to provide confidence in project delivery by ensuring that risks are managed proactively and effectively throughout the engagement.

In terms of process, CGI involves several key steps to ensure a smooth onboarding and knowledge transfer. Here are the main components:

Kick-off Meeting: A kick-off meeting is held with the CGI owner, the person in charge of the project, and if necessary, the CGI representative. This meeting aims to present relevant contextual elements, stakeholder expectations, and to identify contributing resources.

Knowledge Transfer: In the event of a resource replacement, CGI has a structured approach to minimize the impact on the project. Training and Onboarding: CGI employs a bootcamp-type training path to ensure that new advisors understand and master the specific elements of the agile approach. This training is designed to align new resources with the project requirements and expectations.

Continuous Monitoring: Periodic meetings among CGI advisors are held to monitor progress and provide an overall vision and management of the interventions, ensuring that all team members are aligned and informed.

Role 1: Agile Readiness Assessment
Provide an outline of the Proponent’s approach to conducting an Agile Readiness Assessment.
CGI has conducted numerous maturity assessments. The Agile Readiness Assessment is structured in two tiers:
Basic Assessment (Steps 1–3): Evaluates current Agile maturity.
Advanced Assessment (Steps 1–7): Assesses maturity and provides a roadmap for evolution.
The assessment process includes the following steps:
Document Review:

CGI requests and reviews a variety of process documents. These may include, but are not limited to: SDLC documentation, project management processes, testing procedures, sample test plans, architectural diagrams, infrastructure and environment schematics, and any other materials deemed relevant by CGI and the client. This review typically takes 1–2 weeks, depending on the volume of documentation.
Leadership Alignment:

CGI meets with leadership to clarify the desired outcomes of the assessment, determine whether an Agile-at-scale approach is appropriate, and identify key stakeholders to be interviewed. These stakeholders may include representatives from Executive Leadership, Marketing/Sales, IT Infrastructure, Architecture, Development, QA/QE, and Project Management.
Interviews and Maturity Scoring:
CGI conducts interviews with the identified stakeholders. Using a Maturity Assessment Framework, CGI assigns a maturity score across several categories. The scoring model ranges from 1 to 5:
1 = Initial
2 = Managed
3 = Defined
4 = Enabled
5 = Optimizing
Current State Documentation:
CGI documents the current state of Agile maturity and reviews it with the client. Feedback is incorporated to ensure accuracy and completeness.
Future State and Recommendations:
Based on the current state, CGI proposes a potential future state, including detailed recommendations and a realistic timeline for achieving it.
Client Decision:
The client reviews the recommendations and selects which ones to adopt.
Transformation Plan:
CGI develops a tailored transformation plan to evolve Agile practices—or Agile at scale—based on the client’s selected outcomes.
B. Provide an example of a successful agile implementation based on a readiness assessment.
Outline the approach, what the Proponent delivered, and its impact for the client.

One of CGI’s first Agile Maturity Assessments was conducted for TransLink in Vancouver. At the time, TransLink’s Business Technology Services (BTS) division had a five-year track record of delivering projects late and over budget. The organization was considering outsourcing its technology functions.

CGI conducted a maturity assessment and, based on the findings, delivered a set of recommendations—all of which were accepted by TransLink. Following this, CGI provided Agile training to the entire BTS group.

CGI was then contracted to lead the Agile transformation of BTS. The department was reorganized into 16 Scrum teams and 4 Kanban teams, and the transformation was executed in four waves. Some teams were already mid-project, including one working on a machine learning tool that was behind schedule and at risk of running out of funding within four months. BTS would have considered a three-month delivery a success. The team delivered in ten weeks, just two weeks behind the ideal target. The next iteration was delivered on time and on budget, followed by nine successful deliveries in ten months, all on time and within budget.

Later, BTS initiated a project to replace its on-premises data warehouse with a cloud-based solution using Databricks. This was their first distributed project, involving teams in Calgary, Toronto, and Vancouver. Despite the complexity, the team delivered the new data warehouse in 11 weeks, with no loss of functionality and zero downtime—a significant improvement over the original 26-week estimate using a traditional waterfall approach.
Since then, TransLink has continued to evolve its Agile practices. The organization now routinely delivers projects on time and on budget, with delays being the exception rather than the norm.

CGI continues to support Agile and Agile-at-scale transformations, with a strong focus on the SAFe framework. However, CGI is also experienced with other frameworks and is fully capable of designing and executing transformations using models such as the Product Operating Model, LeSS, and DAD.

When clients operate with a mix of internal and external development teams, CGI recommends adopting an Agile-at-Scale framework. A key component of this model is the establishment of an Agile Program Management Office (APMO) within an Agile Release Train (ART). The APMO provides:
Coordination across Agile and non-Agile teams

3. Approach to Agile Readiness Assessment for Clients with External Vendors Using a Hybrid Approach
CGI recognizes several common hybrid delivery scenarios and tailors its recommendations accordingly:
Scenario 1: Internal and External Teams (Some Agile, Some Not)
CGI recommends the Agile-at-Scale model with an APMO.
Non-Agile teams often cannot meet the standard two-week iteration cadence. The System Team negotiates a delivery frequency (e.g., every second or third iteration).
Deliveries are synchronized with Agile sprint completions to maintain integration cadence and minimize disruption.
Scenario 2: All Teams Are External Vendors (Mixed Methodologies)
The same Agile-at-Scale structure is applied.
Vendors are responsible for functional testing.
The client uses automated acceptance testing, developed by internal teams, to validate vendor deliverables and ensure alignment with business requirements.
Scenario 3: Internal Teams Augmented by Vendor Staff or Multiple Vendors
Standard Agile or Agile-at-Scale practices are used.
Team members are fully integrated and identify with their Agile teams rather than their vendor affiliation.
This promotes shared ownership and accountability for outcomes, rather than vendor-specific deliverables.
4. Proven Success and Scalability

These structures have been successfully implemented across numerous CGI client organizations. In large enterprises, even internal dependencies outside the immediate program are treated as vendor relationships to ensure clarity, accountability, and integration discipline.

B. Outline the approach to managing product backlog to delivery.

CGI's approach to managing the product backlog to delivery involves several key practices that ensure effective prioritization, collaboration, and adaptability throughout the Agile process. Here are the main components of this approach:
1. Product Backlog Management

Creation and Maintenance: The product backlog is a prioritized list of project requirements or features that serves as the primary source of work for the Agile team. The Product Owner is responsible for maintaining the backlog, ensuring it reflects the most current project needs and priorities 1 2.
2. Sprint Planning

Selection of User Stories: At the start of each sprint, the Product Owner and Scrum Team select an appropriate number of user stories from the product backlog to create the sprint backlog. This selection is based on the team's average velocity and the estimated level of effort for each story 3.

Planning Meetings: The Product Owner, Scrum Master, and Agile team hold a planning meeting at the beginning of each sprint to review and validate estimates, design the approach for delivery, and self-assign tasks 4 2.
3. Daily Stand-up Meetings

Progress Updates: Daily stand-up meetings, also known as daily scrums, are conducted to promote transparency and communication within the Agile team. Team members share progress, discuss obstacles, and plan their work for the day, ensuring alignment and collaboration 1.
4. Stakeholder Engagement

Regular Reviews: Stakeholders are actively involved throughout the Agile process, participating in regular reviews and providing feedback to ensure alignment with project goals and objectives. This engagement helps in adjusting priorities based on stakeholder input 1.
5. Adaptability and Flexibility

Embracing Change: CGI emphasizes the Agile principle of embracing change, acknowledging that requirements may evolve. The Product Owner can reprioritize the backlog based on feedback from stakeholders and the Scrum team 4 5.
6. Sprint Retrospectives and Reviews

Feedback Mechanisms: Sprint retrospectives provide feedback from the Scrum team on potential improvements to story sizing, wording, and acceptance criteria. Sprint reviews at the conclusion of each sprint allow stakeholders to provide feedback on solution priorities, which may lead to changes in the order of user stories in the backlog for future sprints 2.
7. Continuous Refinement

Ongoing Backlog Refinement: As the project progresses, the backlog is continuously refined to ensure that user stories are well-defined and sized for upcoming sprints. This ongoing refinement helps maintain a steady flow of work for the Scrum teams.
By following this structured approach, CGI effectively manages the product backlog to ensure timely delivery and alignment with project objectives.

B. Provide an example of a successful agile implementation. Outline the approach, what was delivered, and its impact for the client.

CGI transformed TransLink, in Vancouver, from a pure Waterfall model to fully Agile. They were consistently late with projects and often over budget. Initially, TransLink believed they had a testing issue. However, during a Test Maturity Assessment, it became clear that there were broader issues with the SDLC and that Agile could address many of them. All of the detailed recommendations in the assessment were accepted, most of which advocated for the adoption of Agile. First, the Agile structure was designed around their desired outcomes and the products they were delivering. They had several customer-facing products and several internal systems. Once the system was designed, teams were formed and trained in foundational Agile practices, with additional training tailored to their specific delivery models—Scrum or Kanban, as both were used at TransLink. The organization is hierarchical and unionized, which is not typically conducive to Agile. As a result, several negotiations were required to ensure collective agreements were respected. Here’s a comprehensive overview of CGI's processes, tools, and documentation practices related to risk management, scope adjustments, tool selection, and project documentation:
a) Process for Identifying and Mitigating Risk
CGI utilizes the SAFe Agile risk management technique known as ROAM, which stands for Resolve, Own, Accept, and Mitigate. This process involves:
Resolve: Identifying risks and taking actions to ensure they do not become issues.
Own: Assigning an owner to monitor the risk and take action if it arises.
Accept: Acknowledging risks that cannot be avoided and preparing to address them if they become issues.
Mitigate: Creating and executing a plan to reduce the impact of risks if they materialize.
This approach focuses on program-level or cross-team risks, while individual teams are responsible for managing their own risks.
b) Handling Changes or Adjustments to Scope
In an agile environment, changes in requirements and scope are expected. CGI manages this through:
Negotiation: Teams negotiate what can be delayed to accommodate new work, reflecting changes in the backlog.

Capacity Management: If scope increases without extending the delivery date, new teams may be formed to handle the additional work. However, adding resources to existing teams is generally discouraged due to potential negative impacts on velocity.
c) Choosing Tools for Engagement
Tools are selected based on the following criteria:
Fit-for-Purpose: Existing enterprise tools are preferred if they meet the teams' needs.
Open Source Preference: When acceptable, open-source tools are favored for their cost-effectiveness and industry-standard status in agile practices.

Role 5: Release Management
ALC is seeking Proponents that can provide advisory services related to creating structured governance, process optimization, and support for Agile, Waterfall, and hybrid release methodologies.
A. Release Strategy & Governance
i. Outline experience and approach in the following areas:
a) Creating release governance frameworks that accommodate Agile, Waterfall, and hybrid delivery models.
b) Creating release approval processes to ensure compliance with business objectives and regulatory requirements.
c) Ensuring version control and deployment readiness assessments.
ii. Provide two (2) examples of how the Proponent has supported other companies in developing the above release strategy and governance.

a) Creating Release Governance Frameworks CGI developed the Factory Release Governance Model for a global investment bank, which was designed to manage multiple solutions across hundreds of applications. This framework accommodates Agile, Waterfall, and hybrid delivery models, ensuring compliance with various regulatory requirements. It outlines processes for each stage of the release, identifies involved roles, and includes a communication plan for team interactions. Additionally, it addresses post-implementation support, such as incident management and defect resolution, providing a repeatable and scalable methodology for diverse delivery environments.

b) Creating Release Approval Processes To ensure compliance with business objectives and regulatory requirements, CGI created multiple release templates that define each step of the release lifecycle. These templates specify approval roles, including implementers, change managers, and business approvers, and are implemented using ServiceNow for automation and traceability. Each release requires validation of User Acceptance Testing (UAT) completion and formal business sign-off before production deployment, enhancing compliance and audit readiness.

c) Ensuring Version Control and Deployment Readiness Assessments CGI integrated existing version control systems, such as GitHub, and deployment readiness assessments using SonarQube into the release approval process. This integration requires a release link to specified versions and evidence of SonarQube results to ensure only high-quality, tested code is promoted to production. This approach enhances transparency and accountability in the release pipeline and supports continuous improvement through measurable quality indicators.
Examples of Supporting Other Companies

Global Investment Bank: CGI implemented the Factory Release Governance Model, which managed multiple solutions across hundreds of applications, ensuring compliance with regulatory requirements while supporting various delivery models. This model facilitated seamless integration with existing workflows and provided a structured approach to governance.

ServiceNow Implementation: CGI developed structured release templates and processes for a client, automating the release lifecycle through ServiceNow. This ensured that all releases met compliance standards and business expectations, significantly improving audit readiness and reducing risks associated with the release process.
By leveraging these structured governance frameworks and processes, CGI effectively supports organizations in optimizing their release strategies across Agile, Waterfall, and hybrid methodologies.
B. Hybrid Release Management
i. Outline experience and approach in the following areas:
a) Integrating Agile and Waterfall methodologies into a cohesive release strategy.
b) Creating transition models for organizations evolving from Waterfall to Agile-based releases.
c) Blending iterative deployments within milestone-based releases.
d) Supporting hybrid environment processes, enabling teams to deliver based on project-specific requirements.
ii. Provide two (2) examples of how the Proponent has supported other companies in developing hybrid release management.
a) Integrating Agile and Waterfall Methodologies

CGI has successfully integrated Agile and Waterfall methodologies into a cohesive release strategy. This involved transitioning from a traditional Waterfall approach, which utilized SharePoint for requirements and design documentation, to a more Agile method using Jira and sprints. The integration was carefully planned to ensure continuity and alignment across both methodologies, allowing teams to operate within their preferred frameworks while maintaining a unified delivery cadence. This approach minimized disruption and effectively managed dependencies between Agile and Waterfall teams.
b) Creating Transition Models for Organizations Evolving from Waterfall to Agile

CGI developed transition models that included clear guidance for teams on how and when to shift from Waterfall to Agile-based releases. The model involved winding down Waterfall work at key milestones, followed by a cutover to Agile for subsequent phases. This phased approach allowed teams to adapt gradually while maintaining delivery momentum. Communication plans and training were implemented to support the transition and reduce resistance to change.
c) Blending Iterative Deployments within Milestone-Based Releases

The transition from Application Lifecycle Management (ALM) defects and change requests to Jira-managed defects and user stories allowed for iterative delivery within broader milestone-based planning. Agile sprints were aligned with key delivery checkpoints, ensuring that incremental progress supported overall project timelines. This hybrid approach enabled faster feedback loops while still meeting structured release commitments.
d) Supporting Hybrid Environment Processes

CGI's hybrid model supports teams working in both Agile and Waterfall environments by allowing them to follow project-specific processes while contributing to a shared release plan. This flexibility ensures that each team can operate effectively within its own context. Governance and reporting structures were adapted to accommodate both delivery styles, ensuring transparency and accountability across the entire program.
Examples of Supporting Other Companies

Transition for a Major Client: CGI facilitated the transition from Waterfall to Agile for a significant client by implementing a phased approach. This included winding down Waterfall projects at key milestones and transitioning to Agile methodologies, supported by communication plans and training to ease the change process.

Hybrid Release Management for a Government Agency: CGI supported a government agency in developing a hybrid release management strategy that blended iterative deployments with milestone-based releases. This involved aligning Agile sprints with key delivery checkpoints, allowing for faster feedback while still adhering to structured release commitments.
By leveraging these strategies and experiences, CGI effectively supports organizations in managing hybrid release environments, ensuring successful integration of Agile and Waterfall methodologies.
C. Agile Release Support
i. Outline experience and approach in the following areas:
a) Creating CI/CD (Continuous Integration / Continuous Deployment) best practices for fast-paced Agile environments.
b) Creating cross-functional collaboration for iterative releases, ensuring minimal downtime.
c) Sprint-Based Releases, Rolling Deployments, and Feature Flags for controlled deployment.
ii. Provide two (2) examples of how the Proponent has supported other companies in developing the above agile release support.
a) Creating CI/CD Best Practices for Fast-Paced Agile Environments

CGI established a dedicated Change and Release team to support various application teams in navigating the release process after creating the Factory model. This team aligned Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) practices with Agile delivery timelines to ensure rapid and reliable deployments. They provided hands-on guidance to optimize integration and deployment pipelines for speed and quality, which helped reduce manual intervention and increased deployment frequency.
b) Creating Cross-Functional Collaboration for Iterative Releases

The Change and Release team collaborated closely with development, testing, and operations teams to coordinate releases effectively. This collaboration included post-deployment monitoring to identify issues or required changes, which were then routed back to the development and testing teams for resolution. This feedback loop ensured continuous improvement and minimized service disruption during iterative releases.
c) Sprint-Based Releases, Rolling Deployments, and Feature Flags for Controlled Deployment

CGI's release process supported sprint-based delivery, allowing for incremental improvements to be deployed regularly. Rolling deployments were utilized to reduce risk and ensure stability during production updates. Additionally, feature flags were implemented to enable controlled feature rollouts and quick rollbacks if necessary. This approach allowed teams to deliver value continuously while maintaining system reliability.
Examples of Supporting Other Companies

Agile Transformation for a Major Client: CGI supported a significant client in implementing CI/CD best practices tailored for fast-paced Agile environments. The Change and Release team worked closely with the client’s teams to optimize their deployment pipelines, resulting in increased deployment frequency and reduced manual intervention.

Cross-Functional Collaboration for a Government Agency: CGI facilitated cross-functional collaboration for a government agency by establishing a structured feedback loop between development, testing, and operations teams. This collaboration minimized downtime during iterative releases and ensured that issues were promptly addressed in subsequent release cycles.
By leveraging these strategies and experiences, CGI effectively supports organizations in enhancing their Agile release processes, ensuring rapid and reliable delivery of value.

CGI’s Agile Center of Excellence led the orchestration of the Symphony Program, providing end-to-end support in designing and deploying Agile processes, tools, and governance structures. Leaders and teams were equipped with Lean/Agile principles and practices, enabling them to adopt new ways of working and integrate agility into the organizational culture. To drive long-term value, CGI introduced a continuous improvement plan centered on performance measurement, feedback loops, and iterative refinement of processes and tools. Communities of practice were established to support knowledge sharing and role-specific development.

The first iteration of Beneva’s value creation system (SCVB) was successfully launched in January 2024. Since then, the Symphony Train has continued to evolve, reinforcing the Agile framework and enhancing value delivery across the organization.

CGI understands that each client has unique needs, and we tailor our agile approaches accordingly. This includes leveraging the Scaled Agile Framework (SAFe®) for large-scale agile implementations across organizations and complex projects.

We have extensive experience managing agile transformation initiatives and providing coaching and training on agile practices to help clients enhance their agility and competitiveness. Our expertise in SAFe is particularly robust—we have supported clients in adopting SAFe-aligned agile methods for many years and have implemented the SAFe model across a wide range of organizations.

CGI is also a recognized provider of the full SAFe certification training curriculum, supported by a team of over 170 SAFe Program Consultants (SPCs) who are certified to deliver training and guide agile transformations at scale.
f) The fulfillment turnaround time for ramping up resources is typically between two weeks to two months depending on the skillset required, current available resources and prior commitments.
In terms of process, CGI involves several key steps to ensure a smooth onboarding and knowledge transfer. Here are the main components:

1. Kick-off Meeting: A kick-off meeting is held with the CGI owner, the person in charge of the project, and if necessary, the CGI representative. This meeting aims to present relevant contextual elements, stakeholder expectations, and to identify contributing resources.

2. Knowledge Transfer: In the event of a resource replacement, CGI has a structured approach to minimize the impact on the project. This includes promptly notifying management of the required change, assessing the impact, and ensuring a transfer of expertise from the outgoing resource to the incoming one. The outgoing advisor will document their work and provide access to necessary documents for the new resource.

3. Training and Onboarding: CGI employs a bootcamp-type training path to ensure that new advisors understand and master the specific elements of the agile approach. This training is designed to align new resources with the project requirements and expectations.

4. Continuous Monitoring: Periodic meetings among CGI advisors are held to monitor progress and provide an overall vision and management of the interventions, ensuring that all team members are aligned and informed.
This structured transition process is designed to ensure that new resources are effectively integrated into the project, maintaining continuity and minimizing disruptions.

ITEM,55678_38749_0,,B.,"Describe, in detail, the experience your company has providing agile delivery services.  Outline any experience providing agile delivery services related to ALC’s core business.  ",5,"CGI has extensive experience delivering agile services across a variety of industries and organizational contexts. We specialize in implementing scalable frameworks, fostering agile mindsets, and enabling continuous value delivery. For the purpose of this response, we will focus on our engagement with Beneva, where we successfully applied our agile delivery expertise to support a large-scale transformation initiative. The key activities and deliverables from this engagement are summarized below:
1. Establishment of Program Governance Structure
We implemented a comprehensive governance structure with dedicated committees and platforms:
• Vision Committee: Comprised of four Executive Vice Presidents, this committee defines the program’s vision, strategic direction, and priorities.
• Alignment Committee: Includes eight agility ambassadors (Vice Presidents) from various sectors, responsible for aligning the organization with the agility vision.

• Symphony Train Coordination Committee: Oversees the Symphony program and its Agile Release Train (ART). Members include the Program Director (PM), System Architect (SA), Release Train Engineer (RTE), Strategic Agility Advisor, Change Management Advisor, Talent and Culture Advisor, and Directors from the Agility Center of Excellence and Project Office.
2. Implementation of the Symphony Train and SAFe-Inspired Governance Events
The Symphony Train unites contributors from across the organization into twelve agile teams, including:
• Coordination
• Strategy Section
• Portfolio Section
• Delivery Section
• Center of Excellence in Agility (CEA)
• Project Office
• Individual Insurance and Financial Services (AISF)
• Group Insurance
• Property Insurance
• Corporate
• Strategy, Customer Experience, and Marketing
• Business Performance and IT (PATI)
Key governance events include:
• Planning Interval (PI): A time-boxed period (8–12 weeks) for aligning team efforts with strategic goals.
• ART Sync: Regular synchronization meetings to share updates, resolve issues, and maintain alignment.
• Integrated Demos: Frequent demonstrations of product increments to validate progress and gather feedback.
• Inspect & Adapt (I&A): A critical reflection event to assess performance, identify improvements, and define actionable steps for the next PI.
The RTE plays a central role in facilitating these events, supporting team collaboration, and optimizing value delivery across three dimensions:
• Alignment with portfolio objectives and organizational strategy
• Capability building to meet portfolio ambitions
• Execution efficiency to maximize value flow
3. Development of SCVB Processes, Tools, and Governance Frameworks
We designed and documented end-to-end value delivery processes through three core components:
• Strategy: Vision and strategic planning
• Portfolio: Portfolio management
• Delivery: Solution delivery
Work completed:
• Analysis and mapping of existing processes and value chains
• Definition of Agile workflows (e.g., Kanban, Scrum) to connect strategy to execution
• Standardization of planning, prioritization, and execution processes
• Adaptation or acquisition of Agile tools (e.g., Jira)
Deliverables:
• Mapped current and target processes
• Documented Agile workflows
• Established Agile governance and portfolio management tools
4. Agile Portfolio Governance
Work completed:
• Identification and prioritization of initiatives (e.g., using WSJF)
• Definition of Agile governance structures and prioritization criteria
• Processes for identifying delivery vehicles (trains) and transitioning initiatives
• Implementation of portfolio management tools for visibility and tracking
• Regular portfolio review cycles
• Training on Lean Portfolio Management (LPM)
Deliverables:
• Agile governance framework and charter
• Portfolio management tools and dashboards
• Portfolio backlogs
5. Training and Coaching for Agile Leadership
Work completed:
• Training of key leaders in Lean/Agile principles and organizational agility
• Individual and team coaching to build Agile management capabilities
• Support for leaders in integrating agility into strategic and cultural practices
Deliverables:
• Agile training programs for leadership
• Development plans for Agile behaviors
• Agile skills assessment reports
• Ongoing coaching and mentoring frameworks
6. Continuous Improvement and Performance Monitoring
Work completed:
• Implementation of continuous improvement practices (e.g., retrospectives, I&A, demos)
• Collection and analysis of performance metrics (velocity, lead time, cycle time)
• Feedback loop integration to identify and act on improvement opportunities
• Process and tool adjustments based on insights
• Establishment of Communities of Practice (CoPs) for key roles
Deliverables:
• Continuous improvement plan with feedback-based enhancements
• Agile performance dashboards and metrics
• Documentation of learnings and process adjustments
• Periodic reports on Agile framework effectiveness and improvement proposals.

While we have not yet provided agile delivery services directly within ALC’s core business domain, we bring extensive experience in agile transformation and delivery across complex, highly regulated, and customer-centric environments."

ITEM,55760_38778_0,,A.,"Role 1 - Agile Readiness Assessments
A. Provide an outline of the Proponents approach to conducting an Agile Readiness Assessment.
B. Provide an example of a successful agile implementation based on a readiness assessment. Outline the approach, what the Proponent delivered, and its impact for the client.

C. ALC works with several external development teams that use either agile, waterfall or hybrid models for their development approach. As a result, delivery approaches will vary from project to project.
• Provide a description of the Proponents capability and maturity as it relates to Service Delivery Lifecycle (SDLC).
• Outline the approach to conducting an agile readiness assessment for clients utilizing internal and external development teams and associated recommendations.
• Outline the approach to conducting an agile readiness assessment with clients who have external vendors, using a hybrid approach and associated recommendations.
D. Process, Tools and Documentation:
a) Describe the Proponents approach to conducting an agile readiness assessment when coming in to lead a project on behalf of an external client.
b) How would the Proponent communicate and manage expectations with ALC stakeholders throughout the assessment?
c) Describe how the Proponent recommends solutions and tools to improve performance.

d) How does the Proponent handle project documentation and reporting? Provide examples of standard templates, deliverables, and reports you have produced in a past engagement and include a short explanation on what the documentation was used for.

",10,"A. CGI’s Agile Readiness Assessment is delivered in two tiers: Basic (Steps 1–3) and Advanced (Steps 1–7). The Basic Assessment evaluates current Agile maturity, while the Advanced Assessment includes a roadmap for Agile evolution.
1. Document Review: CGI reviews key process documents (e.g., SDLC, testing, architecture) over 1–2 weeks.
2. Leadership Alignment: Meetings clarify assessment goals, Agile-at-scale suitability, and identify stakeholders.
3. Interviews & Scoring: Stakeholders are interviewed and scored using a 1–5 maturity model.
4. Current State: CGI documents and validates the current Agile maturity state with the client.
5. Future State & Recommendations: A proposed future state and timeline are presented.
6. Client Decision: The client selects which recommendations to adopt.
7. Transformation Plan: CGI creates a tailored plan to evolve Agile practices based on selected outcomes.

B. CGI conducted an Agile Maturity Assessment for TransLink’s Business Technology Services (BTS) in Vancouver, which had a history of late, over-budget project deliveries. Facing potential outsourcing, BTS engaged CGI to assess its Agile readiness. CGI’s recommendations were fully accepted, followed by Agile training for the entire BTS team.

CGI then led a full Agile transformation, reorganizing BTS into 16 Scrum and 4 Kanban teams, rolled out in four waves. One team, mid-project on a machine learning tool, was behind schedule and at risk of losing funding. While a three-month delivery was considered a success, the team delivered in ten weeks—just two weeks behind the ideal target. The next iteration was on time and on budget, followed by nine successful deliveries in ten months.

Later, BTS launched a distributed project to replace its on-premises data warehouse with a cloud-based Databricks solution. Despite involving teams across three cities, the project was completed in 11 weeks—far ahead of the original 26-week waterfall estimate—with no downtime or loss of functionality.
Since then, TransLink has consistently delivered projects on time and on budget. CGI continues to support Agile transformations using SAFe, LeSS, DAD, and the Product Operating Model.
C. CGI’s Capability and Maturity in Service Delivery Lifecycle (SDLC)

CGI brings deep expertise and a high level of maturity across the full SDLC, supporting Agile, Waterfall, and hybrid delivery models. Our approach emphasizes flexibility, governance, and business alignment. We have successfully led complex transformations involving internal teams, external vendors, and mixed methodologies, ensuring consistent quality and delivery outcomes.
Agile Readiness Assessment for Clients with Internal and External Teams

For clients with both internal and external development teams, CGI recommends an Agile-at-Scale framework supported by an Agile Program Management Office (APMO) embedded within an Agile Release Train (ART). The APMO ensures:
• Coordination across Agile and non-Agile teams
• Program/project management for non-Agile vendors
• Executive-level reporting in traditional formats
This model is particularly effective when integrating with COTS or SaaS platforms, ensuring alignment and delivery cadence across diverse teams.
D. Agile Readiness Assessment for Clients Using Hybrid Models with External Vendors
CGI tailors its approach based on common hybrid scenarios:
• Scenario 1: Mixed Internal/External Teams (Agile and Non-Agile)
• Use Agile-at-Scale with APMO
• System Team negotiates delivery cadence with non-Agile teams
• Synchronize deliveries with Agile sprints
• Scenario 2: All External Vendors (Mixed Methodologies)
• Apply Agile-at-Scale
• Vendors handle functional testing
• Internal teams develop automated acceptance tests
• Scenario 3: Internal Teams Augmented by Vendors
• Use standard Agile or Agile-at-Scale
• Fully integrate vendor staff into Agile teams
• Promote shared ownership and accountability
Proven Success and Scalability

CGI has implemented these models across large enterprises, treating even internal dependencies as vendor relationships to ensure clarity and integration discipline. This approach enables scalable, predictable delivery across diverse environments.
a) Agile Readiness Assessment Approach

When CGI leads a project on behalf of an external client, the Agile Readiness Assessment is adapted to reflect the delivery structure. If the external client provides delivery teams and ALC provides the environment, CGI focuses on assessing the maturity of those teams and the ALC leadership responsible for product acceptance. If ALC resources are embedded in vendor-led teams, CGI interviews a representative mix of ALC and vendor personnel to understand delivery capabilities, team dynamics, and stakeholder expectations.
b) Communication and Expectation Management
CGI ensures ALC stakeholders are engaged throughout the assessment. Key touchpoints include:
• Current State Validation: ALC reviews and approves maturity scoring.
• Future State Review: ALC provides input on proposed improvements.
• Recommendation Selection: ALC chooses which recommendations to adopt.
Regular updates, collaborative workshops, and transparent reporting ensure alignment and manage expectations effectively.
c) Recommending Solutions and Tools
CGI tailors tool recommendations to the client’s environment and goals. For example:
• Azure DevOps for clients using Microsoft ecosystems
• Jira and Confluence for Agile planning and documentation in open-source environments
Recommendations align with team maturity, infrastructure, and long-term strategy.
d) Documentation and Reporting
CGI emphasizes actionable, audience-specific documentation. Key practices include:
• OKRs: Used to track progress (e.g., “Deliver MVP with 10 features in 3 quarters”)
• Dashboards: Real-time visibility via tools like Jira
• Design Documents: Support development and decision validation
• User Guides & Online Help: Aid onboarding and support
• Technical Data Packages: Include installation guides, configuration manuals, and system architecture overviews
All documentation is stored in accessible platforms like Confluence or SharePoint and tailored for technical teams, business stakeholders, or end users."
ITEM,55760_38779_0,,B.1,"Role 2 - Agile Training and Coaching

ALC is seeking Proponents that can provide individual and team training on how to implement agile principles and practices, problem solving, and value delivery. It may include leadership and executive coaching, e-learning offering, and team based training on agile practices and principles, as well as agile methodologies, process optimization, tools, skills development, and incorporating new technologies. The goal is to support the overall Agile Delivery, Waterfall and Hybrid testing methodologies.
A. Describe, in detail, the experience the Proponent has providing agile training and coaching services. Outline the experience and certifications of your instructors.

B. Provide an outline of the Proponents current training, e-learning, virtual and in-person coaching services. List all courses the Proponent specializes in and outline various delivery methodologies.
C. Outline the following:
a) Proponents approach to agile training services when coming in to lead an agile training project on behalf of an external client.
b) Proponents approach to agile coaching for Leadership and Senior Executives.
c) Checks and controls the Proponent has in place to guarantee the quality of services.
d) How the Proponent conducts a needs assessment to determine the current knowledge base in order to recommend a training program to improve agile delivery.
D. Provide an outline of the pricing models used by the Proponent beyond rate per hour services.
E. Does the Proponent provide train the trainer sessions to support in house delivery of training?

",5,"A. CGI has a mature Agile and SAFe (Scaled Agile Framework) practice, with over two decades of experience delivering Agile training and coaching across industries and organizational sizes. Since the early 2000s—and with significant growth since 2015—CGI has supported hundreds of Agile team transformations and enterprise-level adoptions. Thousands of professionals have completed CGI’s training programs, gaining practical skills in Agile principles, tools, and delivery practices. In the past four years alone, over 1,000 CGI consultants in Canada have been trained and certified in SAFe.
Instructor Experience and Certifications
CGI’s Agile instructors and coaches are highly qualified, combining real-world delivery experience with industry-recognized certifications, including:
• SAFe Program Consultants (SPCs) – Certified to deliver SAFe training and lead transformations
• Scrum Alliance – CSM, CSPO, and CSP certifications
• ICAgile – Certified in Agile coaching, facilitation, and leadership
• PMI-ACP – For instructors with project management and Agile delivery backgrounds
CGI’s coaches bring hands-on experience in Agile transformation leadership, cross-functional team enablement, and scaling Agile practices across complex environments.
B.

CGI offers a dyanmic suite of training, e-learning, virtual, and in-person coaching services designed to support Agile adoption and workforce development. These services are tailored to client needs and aligned with industry best practices.
Training Services

CGI delivers a wide range of Agile training programs, grounded in academic rigor and practical application. All consultants are trained in Agile, with a focus on Scrum and SAFe. Where certification is not required, CGI offers customized training aligned with the client’s culture and goals.
E-Learning Services
CGI’s e-learning platform includes interactive courses on Agile methodologies and tools such as Jira. These self-paced modules provide flexibility and engagement for learners.
Coaching Services

CGI provides coaching for leadership and delivery teams, focusing on Agile practices, collaboration, and strategic thinking. Coaching is often integrated with training to reinforce learning and support real-time application.
Specialized Courses
• Agile Fundamentals (Scrum, SAFe)
• SAFe Certification (Scrum Master, Product Owner)
• Customized Agile Workshops
• Leadership Development
• Collaboration and Team Dynamics
Delivery Methodologies
• Instructor-Led Training: In-person sessions with certified Agile practitioners
• Virtual Training: Live online sessions using video conferencing tools
• E-Learning: Self-paced, interactive modules
• Workshops: Hands-on, scenario-based learning
• Coaching: Personalized support for individuals or teams, often embedded in projects

CGI’s blended approach ensures that training is accessible, relevant, and impactful. By combining structured learning with real-world coaching, CGI helps clients like Atlantic Lottery build sustainable Agile capabilities and achieve strategic outcomes..
C.
a) CGI’s Approach to Agile Training Services

When leading an Agile training project for an external client, CGI begins with an Agile Maturity Assessment to evaluate the current knowledge base and identify training needs. Training programs are then tailored to the client’s goals, team dynamics, and existing Agile maturity. CGI emphasizes that Agile is not a one-size-fits-all model—training is context-specific and aligned with the organization’s strategic objectives. Once training is delivered, CGI recommends embedding Agile coaches to reinforce learning, support adoption, and guide teams through real-world application. This ensures that Agile principles are upheld while allowing flexibility in how teams achieve them.
b) Agile Coaching for Leadership and Senior Executives

CGI believes Agile transformation must be led from the top. Coaching for leadership begins with foundational training, particularly in servant leadership. Executives are then coached through Agile ceremonies such as PI Planning and Product Owner Syncs, especially in SAFe environments. This approach ensures leaders understand their role in enabling Agile success and are equipped to support cultural and operational change.
c) Quality Assurance: Checks and Controls

CGI maintains high-quality service delivery through certified coaches—most are SAFe Program Consultants (SPCs) and many hold additional Agile certifications. Agile and Agile-at-Scale are managed as formal practices within CGI, with regular Synergy Reviews where coaches share lessons learned and peer-review each other’s engagements. This collaborative model ensures consistency, continuous improvement, and high standards across all training and coaching services.
d) Needs Assessment and Training Program Design

CGI’s Agile Maturity Assessment includes targeted questions to evaluate team knowledge, delivery practices, and organizational readiness. Based on this, CGI designs a training roadmap aligned with desired outcomes. Coaches continuously assess team progress and recommend incremental, workshop-based training using real project artifacts (e.g., epics, stories, tasks). This ensures training is relevant, timely, and directly applicable, supporting continuous learning and Agile maturity growth.
D.

CGI typically uses a Time and Materials pricing model for project delivery but is open to alternative models. If ALC proposes a different structure, CGI will evaluate it based on project scope, deliverables, and market value. Fixed Fee contracts, including contingency, have been used in similar engagements. Additionally, CGI offers a Managed Services pricing model if preferred. All pricing approaches are assessed to ensure fair value, alignment with requirements, and appropriate return on investment.
E.

Yes, CGI provides train-the-trainer sessions to support in-house delivery. Change Agents, Scrum Masters, and Kanban Team Leads are identified and trained to coach others. CGI coaches initially guide Agile practices, then gradually step back as internal leaders gain confidence. This approach ensures a smooth transition, enabling long-term sustainability and self-sufficiency in Agile delivery across all levels, including leadership and executive teams."
ITEM,55760_167226_0,,B.2,"Role 2 - continued
F. Describe how the Proponent stays on top of new technologies and emerging trends related to agile delivery. How is this transitioned into your training programs or offerings, and the client?
G. What is the Proponents approach to knowledge transfer and training within your organization?
H. Does the Proponent create customized training materials specific to clients needs?
I. What is the Proponent’s lead time to provide individual and team training sessions?",5,"F.

CGI employs a proactive and integrated approach to staying current with new technologies and emerging trends in Agile delivery. This is rooted in a strong culture of continuous learning, where consultants are encouraged to pursue certifications and stay informed on evolving Agile practices. CGI manages the transition from engagement completion to operations by aligning with ALC’s operational strategy and ensuring seamless collaboration between development and operations teams. The transition approach depends on whether ALC assigns support responsibilities to a separate operations team or retains them within the development teams.

If a separate support team is designated, CGI recommends early engagement of the Operations Team during the development phase. This ensures they are familiar with the solution and deployment process. CGI typically advocates for DevOps functions to reside within the Operations Team, allowing them to manage deployments and operational considerations effectively.

A comprehensive knowledge base is developed collaboratively between development and operations teams to support ongoing maintenance and issue resolution. If professional services are required for production deployment, these are handled by the Operations Team to ensure operational continuity.

Support tickets are managed through a structured process. If enhancements are needed, tickets are converted into user stories or tasks and added to the development backlog, enabling continuous improvement.

If development teams are responsible for support, no formal hand-off is required. A helpdesk handles basic support and triages tickets, which are then added to the development backlog. This embeds DevOps within the development cycle and ensures rapid response and resolution.
F.
To ensure effective collaboration among cross-functional teams using Agile, Waterfall, or hybrid models, CGI applies a flexible, structured approach tailored to each project’s context.

CGI recommends adopting an Agile-at-Scale framework to unify delivery across diverse teams. This model integrates external teams—regardless of methodology—into a cohesive delivery structure. When external teams are fully accountable for delivery and testing, ALC conducts acceptance testing to validate outcomes and ensure alignment with user expectations.

Agile external teams are integrated similarly to internal ALC teams, promoting consistency and collaboration. For non-Agile teams, CGI introduces an Agile Project Management Office (APMO) within the Agile-at-Scale framework. The APMO provides project and program management support, ensuring non-Agile teams are effectively coordinated within the broader delivery process.

Recognizing that non-Agile teams may not follow a two-week sprint cadence, CGI negotiates delivery schedules using a “harmonic” model. This allows for integration every second or third sprint, maintaining predictability and reducing integration risks.

To foster collaboration, CGI emphasizes open communication through regular sync meetings, joint planning sessions, and shared tracking tools. These practices ensure alignment, transparency, and a shared commitment to project goals.
Through these strategies, CGI enables seamless collaboration across varied delivery models, ensuring successful project outcomes.

All teams involved in the program, regardless of origin, are treated as part of a unified delivery organization. External vendors are considered clients of the program, ensuring clarity in roles and expectations while fostering alignment toward shared goals.

To manage diverse delivery models, CGI employs an Agile-at-Scale framework that accommodates both Agile and non-Agile teams. This framework enables seamless integration of external vendors into the delivery process. Agile coaches are assigned to support external teams, helping them adopt Agile practices and align with project objectives.

For hybrid environments, CGI recommends establishing an Agile Project Management Office (APMO). The APMO provides oversight and coordination for non-Agile teams, ensuring their work aligns with Agile delivery cycles. Delivery schedules are negotiated using a “harmonic” model, allowing non-Agile outputs to integrate predictably with Agile sprints.

Continuous feedback is a cornerstone of CGI’s approach. User interactions and stakeholder input are captured throughout the engagement to validate deliverables and refine processes. This ensures that all teams—internal or external—remain focused on delivering value.

Ultimately, CGI’s strategy emphasizes collaboration, transparency, and adaptability. By aligning all contributors under a shared framework and focusing on outcomes, CGI ensures that hybrid delivery environments are productive, cohesive, and capable of delivering high-quality results.
H.
a) Risk Identification and Mitigation

CGI uses the SAFe Agile ROAM technique—Resolve, Own, Accept, Mitigate—to manage risks. Program-level risks are addressed collaboratively, while team-level risks are managed locally. Risks are logged, reviewed regularly, and assigned owners to ensure accountability and timely action.
b) Managing Scope Changes

In Agile, scope changes are expected. CGI handles them through backlog reprioritization and negotiation. If new work is introduced, teams assess what can be deferred. If delivery timelines remain fixed, additional teams may be formed to absorb the increased workload, though adding members to existing teams is avoided to preserve velocity and cohesion.
c) Tool Selection

Tool selection is based on fitness for purpose. CGI prefers existing enterprise tools when suitable, and favors open-source solutions for cost-effectiveness and flexibility. If necessary, Commercial Off-The-Shelf (COTS) tools are recommended. CGI remains tool-agnostic, focusing on tools that best support the client’s goals and delivery model.
d) Documentation and Reporting

CGI aligns documentation with Agile principles—producing only what is necessary. Design documents are maintained, while test plans are replaced by test-first approaches like Behavior-Driven Development (BDD). End-user guides and Technical Data Packages are created as needed.

For reporting, tools like Jira and Confluence are used to automate real-time metrics collection. Objectives and Key Results (OKRs) are tracked through dashboards. For executive audiences, Agile data is translated into traditional reporting formats using BI tools or project managers to ensure clarity and alignment.

This comprehensive approach ensures that CGI engagements are well-documented, risks are proactively managed, scope changes are handled efficiently, and tools are selected to maximize value and delivery effectiveness."

This collaboration minimized downtime during iterative releases and ensured that issues were promptly addressed in subsequent release cycles.
By leveraging these strategies and experiences, CGI effectively supports organizations in enhancing their Agile release processes, ensuring rapid and reliable delivery of value."

ITEM,55679_38751_0,,A.,"Does the Proponent, regardless of size, have a data privacy officer or equivalent position responsible for leading data privacy initiatives? If applicable, provide the title and list the responsibilities. ",5,"CGI has a designated Chief Privacy Officer (CPO) responsible for leading data privacy initiatives. The CPO oversees company-wide privacy policies and procedures, as well as compliance with data protection regulations.
Additionally, CGI has a network of Data Protection Officers and Strategic Business Unit Privacy Business Partners who assist in these efforts.
Responsibilities of the Chief Privacy Officer and the Data Protection Team:
Monitor compliance with CGI's privacy policies and processes.
Provide guidance, direction, and training regarding CGI's privacy policies and industry best practices.
Contribute to the ongoing development and enhancement of CGI's privacy program.
Promote and foster a culture of data protection excellence within CGI.
Stay current on evolving privacy regulations and industry standards.
The CPO reports directly to the Executive Vice-President, Legal and Economic Affairs, and Corporate Secretary"
ITEM,55679_38752_0,,B.,"Does the Proponent, regardless of its size, have any policies, standards, and guidelines relating to data privacy and the protection of personal information?

If applicable, provide the title and summary of each policy, standard, or guideline that your organization has created relating to privacy and security. As an alternative to providing a summary, your organization may submit a copy of the policy, standard, or guideline for review. If your organization does not have formal policies, standards, or guidelines, please describe any practices or measures your organization has in place to protect data privacy and personal information.
",5,"CGI has established Information Security Policies, Standards, and Specifications that align with industry-recognized codes of practice for information security controls, such as ISO 27002:2013.
Summary of Policies, Standards, and Guidelines:

Information Security Policy: This policy sets the direction for the consistent management of CGI's security risks and provides guidance for establishing security controls to protect both CGI and client information.

Privacy Protection Schedule: This document outlines the commitments and responsibilities regarding the protection of personal information and data privacy, ensuring compliance with relevant laws and regulations.
Data Classification Security Requirements: This standard ensures that all data at rest, including backups, remains secure and compliant with applicable regulations.
CGI also implements a many-tiered approach to data security, ensuring the privacy, security, and protection of client data during projects and within the solutions provided."

ITEM,55679_38753_0,,C.,"Does the Proponent, regardless of size, have a breach response process? Provide details on what your organization would do if it were discovered that your employee(s) were accessing, using, or disclosing ALC confidential information without permission. ",5,"CGI has a breach response process in place. The organization implements a global security incident management process designed to handle all phases of a security incident, including breaches involving confidential information.
Breach Response Process:
Incident Notification: Upon discovering unauthorized access, use, or disclosure of ALC confidential information, the CGI Account Manager will immediately inform the relevant parties.
Incident Management Team Mobilization: An incident manager will be assigned, and a team will be mobilized to contain the breach and gather relevant data for investigation.
Assessment and Prioritization: The incident will be assessed and prioritized according to established standards to ensure timely resolution.
Evidence Collection: CGI will ensure the collection and preservation of evidence throughout the incident management process.
Communication: CGI will provide security incident notifications and status updates to clients, authorities, and affected individuals as required by local legislation and client contracts.
Post-Incident Review: After the incident is resolved, a review will be conducted to evaluate the response and improve future incident management processes."
