2.2 Step I – Mandatory Submission Requirements
Step I will consist of a review to determine which proposals comply with all of the mandatory submission
requirements. If a proposal fails to satisfy all of the mandatory submission requirements, the Province will
issue the Proponent a rectification notice identifying the deficiencies and providing the Proponent an
opportunity to rectify the deficiencies. If the Proponent fails to satisfy the mandatory submission
requirements within the Rectification Period, its proposal will be excluded from further consideration. The
Rectification Period will begin to run from the date that the Province issues a rectification notice to the
Proponent. The mandatory submission requirements are as follows:
2.2.1 Submission Form (Appendix B)
Each proposal MUST include a completed Response Form 1: Submission Form (Appendix B) signed by an
authorized representative of the Proponent.
2.2.2 Submission Pricing Form (Appendix C)
Each proposal MUST include a Response Form 2: Submission Pricing Form (Appendix C) completed
according to the instructions contained in the form.
2.2.3 Attestations Form (Appendix I)
Each proposal MUST include a completed Response Form 3: Attestation Form (Appendix I) signed by an
authorized representative of the Proponent.
2.2.4 Vendor, Technical, Security and Business Requirements Form (Appendix J)
Each proposal MUST include a completed Response Form 4: Vendor, Technical, Security and Business
Requirements form (Appendix J).
When responding to the mandatory requirements on the “Mandatory” tab:
• Proponents MUST indicate “Yes” or “No” in the “Meets Requirement” Column C.
• All Mandatory requirements MUST be met for the proposal to be given further consideration.
• Failure to provide a response in the “Meets Requirement” Column C, or not indicating “Yes” will
result in the proposal being disqualified from further consideration.
When responding to the scored requirements on the “Vendor”, “Technical”, “Security” and “Business”
tabs:
• Column A - #: Indicates the criteria reference number.
• Column B – Requirement Name: Indicates the name of the scored requirement.
• Column C – Criteria: Describes the rated requirement.
• Column D – Client Priority: Describes the priority the requirement has for the Department.
• Column E – Response: Proponents should describe how the proposed system meets the
requirement. Ambiguity will negatively impact evaluation scores. Comprehensive notes and
examples may add value and consequently the Proponent may score higher. If responses are
lengthy, Proponents may use appendices in their response. Proponents should reference the
requirement tab, category, requirement number and requirement name in their appendices.
2.2.5 Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Form (Appendix K)
Each proposal MUST include a completed Response Form 5: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning
(Appendix K).
2.3 Step II – Evaluation
Step II will consist of the following three sub-steps:
2.3.1 Mandatory Technical Requirements
The Province will review the proposals to determine whether the mandatory technical requirements as
set out in Section C of RFP Particulars (Appendix D) have been met. Questions or queries on the part of
the Province as to whether a proposal has met the mandatory technical requirements will be subject to
the verification and clarification process set out in Section 3.3.4. If the Proponent fails to satisfy the
mandatory technical requirements, its proposal will be excluded from further consideration.
2.3.2 Rated Criteria
The Province will evaluate each qualified proposal on the basis of the rated criteria as set out in Section D
of the RFP Particulars (Appendix D). The following is an overview of the categories and weighting for the
rated criteria of the RFP. Proponents who do not meet a minimum threshold score for a category will not
proceed to the next step of the evaluation process.

A minimum overall score of 3,900 points (65%) MUST be achieved on the Vendor (D1), Technical (D2),
Security (D3) and Business Requirements (D4) (Appendix J) to proceed to Step III Demonstration. Failure
to reach 65% overall on these requirements will disqualify the proposal from further review.
On the respective tabs in the Vendor, Technical, Security and Business Requirement (Appendix J), each
requirement category has been assigned a Total Number of Points Available. Each requirement has been
assigned a weighting and will be rated on a scale of 0-10.
2.3.3 Reference Validation
GNB reserves the right to validate the top ranked proponent's references prior to contract award. If any
information received during these reference calls deems any aspect of the references provided to be
inaccurate, misleading, or contradictory to the information provided in the Vendor's proposal, GNB
reserves the right to take action up to and including disqualification. As such, all references should be
willing to be contacted.
2.4 Step III – Demonstrations Presented by Shortlisted Proponents
At the completion of Step II a maximum of four (4) highest scoring Proponents on D1 – D4 having met the
combined threshold of 65% minimum score will be invited to provide a comprehensive demonstration of
their proposed system and project approach. If multiple Proponents are tied at the fourth-highest score,
all tied Proponents meeting the minimum threshold will be invited to the demonstration step.
The demonstration step is an essential component of the evaluation process and serves as a dynamic
means to assess the practical application of the proposed system and how it aligns with the requirements
of this RFP. Demonstrations will be held virtually and can be scheduled Monday through Friday from 8:15
am to 4:30 pm Atlantic Standard time. The selected Proponents will be given a minimum of ten (10)
business days’ notice to prepare for their scheduled presentation.
Once the four highest-ranking Proponents are identified, SNB will provide the requirements and criteria
for the demonstration. It is intended that demonstrations will be scheduled for a four (4)-hour period, of
which sixty (60) minutes will be used for questions and answers.
Costs related to any responses or presentations are the responsibility of the Proponent. Proponents shall
not be permitted to present new information or adjust proposal content (including price).
There is a total of 2,000 points available for the demonstration, which will be worth 20% of the overall
score.
A minimum score of 65% MUST be achieved on Step III to proceed to Step IV. Failure to reach 65% on the
demonstration will disqualify the Proponent from further consideration.
Proponents with a minimum score of 65% on the Rated Criteria and a minimum score of 65% on the
Demonstration will progress to Step IV – Pricing.
2.5 Step IV– Pricing
Step IV will consist of a scoring of the submitted pricing of qualified proposals in accordance with the price
evaluation set out in the Submission Pricing Form (Appendix C). The evaluation of price will be undertaken
after the evaluation of mandatory submission requirements, mandatory technical requirements, rated
criteria, and demonstrations have been completed. The total price of the implementation and original 10-
year term will be evaluated.
2.6 Step V – Ranking and Contract Negotiations
2.6.1 Ranking of Proponents
After the completion of Step IV, all scores from Step II, Step III, and Step IV will be added together and
each Proponent will be ranked based on its total score. The top-ranked Proponent will receive a written
invitation to enter into direct contract negotiations to finalize an agreement with the Province. Upon
finalization of the Agreement with the Province, the Proponent shall thereafter be known as the
Successful Proponent.
2.6.2 Contract Negotiation Process
Any negotiations will be subject to the process rules contained in the terms and conditions of the RFP
Process (Part 3) and will not constitute a legally binding offer to enter into a contract on the part of the
Province or the Proponent and there will be no legally binding relationship created with any Proponent
prior to the execution of a written agreement. The terms and conditions found in the Form of Agreement
(Appendix A) are to form the basis for commencing negotiations between the Province and the selected
Proponent. Negotiations may include requests by the Province for supporting information from the
Proponent to verify or clarify the information provided in its proposal or to confirm the conclusions
reached in the evaluation, including, but not limited to artificial intelligence functionality vetting,
compliance, etc., and may include requests by the Province for improved pricing or performance terms
from the Proponent.
2.6.3 Time Period for Negotiations
The Province intends to conclude negotiations and finalize an agreement with the top-ranked Proponent
during the Contract Negotiation Period, commencing from the date the Province invites the top-ranked
Proponent to enter negotiations. A Proponent invited to enter into direct contract negotiations should
therefore be prepared to provide requested information in a timely fashion and to conduct its
negotiations expeditiously.
2.6.4 Failure to Enter into Agreement
If the top-ranked Proponent and the Province cannot conclude negotiations and finalize the agreement
for the Deliverables within the Contract Negotiation Period, the Province may, upon notice, discontinue
negotiations with the top-ranked Proponent and may invite the second ranked Proponent to enter into
negotiations. This process shall continue until an agreement is finalized, until there are no more
Proponents remaining that are eligible for negotiations or until the Province elects to cancel the RFP
process.
2.6.5 Notification to Other Proponents
Once an agreement is finalized and executed by the Province with a Proponent, the other Proponents
will be notified in accordance with the Terms and Conditions of the RFP Process (Part 3).

PART 3 – TERMS AND CONDITIONS OF THE RFP PROCESS
3.1 General Information and Instructions
3.1.1 Proponents not to change terminology
Changes to the terminology of this RFP are prohibited
3.1.2 Proponents to Follow Instructions
Proponents should structure their proposals in accordance with the instructions in this RFP. Where
information is requested in this RFP, any response made in a proposal should reference the applicable
section numbers of this RFP.
3.1.3 Language
Proponents may submit their proposal in either of the Province of New Brunswick’s two official languages;
English or French. Proponents are advised that The Province may translate their proposals for evaluation
purposes. The Proponent agrees that it will accept The Province’s translations as being equivalent to their
original proposal. Should a Proponent choose to submit both an English and French copy they MUST
clearly indicate which copy is to be considered the “Original”. If there is a circumstance where there is a
substantive difference between the English and French versions of the proposal, the “Original” will be
considered the official copy for evaluation purposes. All suppliers engaged to deliver services on behalf of
the Government of New Brunswick MUST ensure compliance with the Official Languages Act in the
delivery of those services. For more information, please refer to the Official Languages Act.
3.1.4 No Incorporation by Reference
The entire content of the Proponent’s proposal should be submitted in a fixed form, and the content of
websites or other external documents referred to in the Proponent’s proposal but not attached will not
be considered to form part of its proposal.
3.1.5 References and Past Performance
In the evaluation process, the Province may include information provided by the Proponent’s references
and may also consider the Proponent’s past performance or conduct on previous contracts with the
Province.
3.1.6 Information in RFP Only an Estimate
The Province makes no representation, warranty or guarantee as to the accuracy of the information
contained in this RFP, received from the RFP contact or issued by way of amendment. Any quantities
shown or data, or opinion contained in this RFP or provided by way of amendment are estimates only and
are for the sole purpose of indicating to Proponents the general scale and scope of the Deliverables. It is
the Proponent’s responsibility to obtain all the information necessary to prepare a proposal in response
to this RFP.
3.1.7 Proponents to Bear Their Own Costs
The Proponent shall bear all costs associated with or incurred in the preparation and presentation of its
proposal, including, if applicable, costs incurred for interviews, presentations or demonstrations.
3.1.8 Proposal to be retained by the Province
The Province will not return the proposal or any accompanying documentation submitted by a Proponent.
3.2 Business Registration
Proponents may be required to be registered to carry on business in accordance with applicable laws. For
information on the business registration requirements of the Corporate Registry of Service New
Brunswick, please consult:
https://www.pxw1.snb.ca/snb7001/e/2000/2500e.asp
The status of a Proponent’s business registration does not preclude the submission of a proposal in
response to this RFP. A proposal can be accepted for evaluation, regardless of (i) whether the company
is registered, or (ii) whether its business registration is in good standing.
3.3 Communication after Issuance of RFP
3.3.1 Proponents to Review RFP
Proponents shall promptly examine all of the documents comprising this RFP, and
a) report any errors, omissions, or ambiguities; and
b) direct questions or seek additional information
in writing by email to the RFP Contact on or before the Deadline for Questions. No such communications
are to be directed to anyone other than the RFP Contact. The Province is under no obligation to provide
additional information, and the Province will not be responsible for any information provided by or
obtained from any source other than the RFP Contact. It is the responsibility of the Proponent to seek
clarification from the RFP Contact on any matter it considers to be unclear. The Province will not be
responsible for any misunderstanding on the part of the Proponent concerning this RFP or its process.
3.3.2 All New Information to Proponents by Way of Amendment
This RFP may be amended only by addendum in accordance with this section. If the Province, for any
reason, determines that it is necessary to provide additional information relating to this RFP, such
information will be communicated by addendum on the New Brunswick Opportunities Network (NBON).
Each addendum forms an integral part of this RFP and may contain important information, including
significant changes to this RFP. Proponents are responsible for obtaining all amendments issued by the
Province and will be deemed to have read all posted amendments.
3.3.3 Post-Deadline Amendment and Extension of Submission Deadline
If the Province determines that it is necessary to issue an addendum after the Deadline for Issuing
Amendments, the Province may extend the Submission Deadline for a reasonable period of time.
3.3.4 Verify and Clarify
During the evaluation process, the Province may request further information from the Proponent or third
parties in order to verify or clarify the information provided in the Proponent’s proposal, including but not
limited to clarification with respect to whether a proposal meets the mandatory technical requirements
set out in Section C of the RFP Particulars (Appendix D). The Province may revisit and re-evaluate the
Proponent’s response or ranking on the basis of any such information.
3.4 Notification and Debriefing
3.4.1 Notification of Outcome of Procurement Process
Once an agreement is executed by the Province with a Proponent, notification of the outcome of the
procurement process will be posted on the New Brunswick Opportunities Network (NBON).
3.4.2 Debriefing
Proponents may request a debriefing after notification of the outcome of the procurement process. All
requests MUST be in writing to the RFP Contact and MUST be made within sixty (60) days of notification
of the outcome of the procurement process. The intent of the debriefing information session is to aid the
Proponent in presenting a better proposal in subsequent procurement opportunities. Any debriefing
provided is not for the purpose of providing an opportunity to challenge the procurement process or its
outcome.
3.5 Conflict of Interest and Prohibited Conduct
3.5.1 Conflict of Interest
The Province may disqualify a Proponent for any conduct, situation or circumstance, determined by the
Province, in its sole and absolute discretion, to constitute a Conflict of Interest. For the purposes of this
Section, “Conflict of Interest” has the meaning ascribed to it in the Submission Form (Appendix B).
3.5.2 Disqualification for Prohibited Conduct
The Province may disqualify a Proponent, rescind an invitation to negotiate or terminate an agreement
entered into if the Province, in its sole and absolute discretion, determines that the Proponent has
engaged in any conduct prohibited by this RFP.
3.5.3 Prohibited Proponent Communications
A Proponent shall not engage in any communications that could constitute a Conflict of Interest and MUST
take note of the Conflict of Interest declaration set out in the Submission Form (Appendix B).
3.5.4 Proponent not to Communicate with Media
A Proponent may not at any time directly, or indirectly, communicate with the media in relation to this
RFP or any agreement entered into pursuant to this RFP without consent of the Province, and then only
in coordination with the Province.
3.5.5 No Lobbying
A Proponent shall not, in relation to this RFP or the evaluation and selection process, engage directly or
indirectly in any form of political or other lobbying whatsoever to influence the selection of the successful
Proponent.
3.5.6 Illegal or Unethical Conduct
Proponents shall not engage in any illegal business practices, including activities such as bid-rigging, price-
fixing, bribery, fraud, coercion or collusion. Proponents shall not engage in any unethical conduct,
including lobbying, as described above, or other inappropriate communications; offering gifts to any
employees, officers, agents, elected or appointed officials or other representatives of the Province;
submitting proposals containing misrepresentations or other misleading or inaccurate information; or any
other conduct that compromises or may be seen to compromise the competitive process provided for in
this RFP.
3.5.7 Disqualification for Offences
In accordance with sections 33 to 50 of Regulation 2014-93 under the Procurement Act, the Minister
responsible for Service New Brunswick may disqualify a supplier from providing goods and services for
past performance. And, in accordance with sections 51 to 55 of Regulation 2014-93, a supplier who is
guilty of an offence listed in Schedule C of the Regulation is disqualified from providing goods and services
for the corresponding period indicated in Schedule C.
3.6 Confidential Information
3.6.1 Confidential Information of the Province
All information provided by or obtained from the Province in any form in connection with this RFP either
before or after the issuance of this RFP
(a) is the sole property of the Province and MUST be treated as confidential;
(b) is not to be used for any purpose other than replying to this RFP and the performance of the
agreement for the Deliverables;
(c) MUST not be disclosed without prior written authorization from the Province;
(d) MUST be returned by the Proponent to the Province immediately upon request of the Province;
and
(e) Proponents must maintain security standards consistent with security policies of the Province.
These include strict control of access to data and maintaining confidentiality of information gained
while carrying out their duties.
3.6.2 Confidential Information of Proponent
A Proponent should identify any information in its proposal or any accompanying documentation supplied
in confidence for which confidentiality is to be maintained by the Province. The confidentiality of such
information will be maintained by the Province, except as otherwise required by law or by order of a court
or tribunal. Proponents are advised that their proposals will, as necessary, be disclosed, on a confidential
basis, to advisers retained by the Province to advise or assist with the RFP process, including the evaluation
of proposals.
3.6.3 Personal Information
The Right to Information and Protection of Privacy Act, the Personal Health Information Privacy and Access
Act, and other applicable legislations create obligations for the Province and its services providers when
personal information or personal health information is collected, used, or disclosed. Requirements include
limited collections, use, disclosure, and retention of any personal information or personal health
information. The Proponent MUST comply with the requirements of the Personal Health Information
Privacy and Access Act and the Right to Information and Protection of Privacy Act of the Province of New
Brunswick and other applicable legislations during the contractual term.
3.7 Procurement Process Non-binding
3.7.1 No Contract A and No Claims
This procurement process is not intended to create or be deemed to create a formal, legally binding
bidding process and shall instead be governed by the law applicable to direct commercial negotiations.
For greater certainty and without limitation, this RFP shall not give rise to any Contract A-based tendering
law duties or any other legal obligations arising out of any process contract or collateral contract.
3.7.2 No Contract until Execution of Written Agreement
This RFP process is intended to identify prospective suppliers for the purposes of negotiating a potential
agreement for the Deliverables. No legal relationship or obligation regarding the procurement of any good
or service shall be created between a Proponent and the Province by this RFP process until the successful
negotiation and execution of a written agreement between a Proponent and the Province for the
acquisition of such goods and/or services.
3.7.3 Non-binding Price Estimates
While the pricing information provided in proposals will be non-binding prior to the execution of a written
agreement, such information will be assessed during the evaluation of the proposals and the ranking of
the Proponents. Any inaccurate, misleading or incomplete information, including withdrawn or altered
pricing, could adversely impact any such evaluation or ranking or the decision of the Province to enter
into an agreement with a Proponent for the Deliverables.
3.7.4 Cancellation
The Province may cancel the RFP process without liability at any time prior to the execution of a written
agreement between the Province and a Proponent.
3.8 Governing Law and Interpretation
These terms and conditions of the RFP Process (Part 3):
(a) are intended to be interpreted broadly and independently (with no particular provision intended
to limit the scope of any other provision);
(b) are non-exhaustive and shall not be construed as intending to limit the pre-existing rights of the
parties to engage in pre-contractual discussions in accordance with the common law governing
direct commercial negotiations; and
(c) are to be governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of the province of New
Brunswick and the federal laws of Canada applicable therein.
3.9 Participation of Eligible Public Sector Entities
By submitting a proposal in response to this RFP, a Proponent irrevocably undertake and agrees that if
successful, and following execution of an agreement with the Province, it will make the specified goods
and/or services available to any public sector entity eligible to participate in this procurement process
upon request by a public sector entity seeking access to those goods and/or services, provided however,
that the Proponent’s obligation to allow participation by other public sector entities does not extend to
circumstances in which the Proponent would have to make capital or operational expenditures specifically
in order to accommodate subsequent requests for goods or services by public sector entities.
The Proponent may only provide the goods and services specified under this RFP to additional entities by
entering into a separate contract with the new entity (“Additional Contract”). The Proponent
acknowledges and agrees that the Province will not be a party to any Additional Contract, nor will the
Province be liable in any respect for any obligation under, or act or omission by a party to, an Additional
Contract.
For the purposes of this section, a public sector entity means any provincial government or provincially
funded entity in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, and Newfoundland and Labrador,
including municipalities, universities, community colleges, school boards, health authorities, housing
authorities, agencies, boards, commissions, and crown corporations. Further, any agreement the
successful Proponent enters into with an eligible public sector entity shall be on the same terms and
conditions, including pricing, and expiry date, contained in the agreement it enters into for the same goods
and /or services with the Province hereunder.

The Justice Services Division is responsible for ensuring transparent and unbiased access to the justice
system in New Brunswick. It provides comprehensive administrative and operational support to all three
levels of court (see below) and supports the judiciary in delivering timely justice and leverages technology
to improve service efficiency and accessibility.
The Court Services Branch supports New Brunswick’s court system (https://www.courtsnb-
coursnb.ca/content/cour/en.html) across eight geographical locations, including the Court of King’s
Bench, Small Claims Court, Probate Court, Bankruptcy and Insolvency Division, Criminal Court and Youth
Justice Court. It manages court attendance, order production, case files, registry services and other
administrative services in support of the judiciary and the public. The branch is also responsible for the
delivery of specialized initiatives, including the Elsipogtog Healing to Wellness Court, Domestic Violence
Court, Family Case Management, Family Law Information Center, Mental Health Docket, and Intimate
Partner Violence Intervention.
The Office of the Registrar supports the Court of Appeal and its judiciary by providing guidance to the
public and lawyers regarding the Rules of Court, order/judgment production, case file management and
other administrative services including conducting hearings as authorized by legislation and the Rules of
Court. This branch serves as the registry for New Brunswick for all bankruptcies and divorces, processes
inter-jurisdictional applications for the establishment of variation of family support orders and processes
all New Brunswick adoptions.
The Office of the Chief Legal Officer provides legal support to the Court of King's Bench and the public for
eight judicial districts. The legal officers are responsible for conducting hearings and adjudicating matters
including but not limited to support enforcement hearings for determination of arrears; Administrative

The Justice Support Services Branch provides strategic and operational support for the technological and
functional processes related to the administration of justice in New Brunswick. Responsibilities include

policy changes; and the establishment and oversight of service level agreements.
The New Brunswick Courts have three levels:
1. The Provincial Court is the entry point for all persons charged with offences under the Criminal
Code or other federal or provincial legislation. The Provincial Court has jurisdiction to try almost
all indictable offences involving adult accused (murder being the main exception), all offences
involving youths under the Youth Criminal Justice Act (ages 12 to 18), and all summary conviction
offences for both adults and youths. Currently the Court consists of a Chief Judge, an Associate
Chief Judge, 23 judges, 2 supernumerary judges and 4 per diem judges.
Provincial Court judges also receive Informations (the documents which contain charges), issue
Search Warrants, Summonses, and Subpoenas, Warrants of Arrest, and conduct Bail Hearings of
accused persons who appear before the Court in custody. In addition to conducting regular Court
sittings on a daily basis.
Provincial Court Judges also hold “Remand Court” on weekends and statutory holidays to allow
persons who have been arrested by the police to be brought before a Judge within 24 hours.
The Provincial Court also has a Mental Health Court in the City of Saint John.

Records Management
Pursuant to the Archives Act, a “record” means (a) correspondence, memoranda, forms, and other papers
and books; (b) maps, plans and charts; (c) photographs, prints and drawings; (d) motion picture films,
microfilms, and video tapes; (e) sound recordings, magnetic tapes, computer cards and other machine
readable records; and (f) all other documentary materials regardless of physical form or characteristics;
(documents).
The duration for which a court record is retained, and its disposal action is governed by a Records
Retention and Disposition Schedule. Court records MUST be authentic, reliable, have integrity and be
useable for as long as they are required according to their Records Retention and Disposition Schedule.
Some records are authorized to be destroyed after their retention period, and others are transferred to
the Archives to be retained in perpetuity.
Though the general rule is that the public has a presumptive right of access to court proceedings and court
records, the Supreme Court of Canada has held that courts do have a supervisory and protecting power
over their records. While ensuring openness, members of the judiciary also have a responsibility to protect
the integrity of the judicial process. The Access to Court Records Guideline
(https://www2.gnb.ca/content/gnb/en/departments/public-safety/justice/content/access-to-court-
records.html) is designed to assist anyone navigating the process of accessing records at Provincial Court
and Court of King’s Bench.

Microsoft Access database, and external scheduling processes in Microsoft Outlook. The legacy case
management systems will be phased out and replaced by the successful Proponent’s system. Information
on the number of databases for each system are included below; the new system does not need to contain
the same number of databases as long as the segregation of data can be achieved through security access
permissions.
The Department would like to implement a central client repository; however, the feasibility and
cost/benefit of merging existing client records will be discussed with the successful Proponent. Pricing
proposals (Appendix C – Submission Pricing Form), “1. Pricing Rated” tab should include data migration of
party records, but should not include costs for merging party records in the data conversion. Proponents
should include their per diem rate for merging party records on Appendix C – Submission Pricing Form,
“3. Per Diem Rates” tab. If after discussions with the successful Proponent, merging party records is
deemed beneficial, merging party records may be invoiced separately as an optional service at the
Department’s discretion.
Justice Information System of New Brunswick (JISNB):
JISNB is used for managing Provincial Court matters and by the Court of King’s Bench for criminal
law cases. Built on SQL server-based data infrastructure, JISNB is divided into separate databases
for adult and youth matters. JISNB is comprised of two-hundred and eighty (280) tables across
three (3) databases as follows:
Database # Tables
Adult 135
Youth 138
Users 7
Documents are maintained in paper format (i.e., not stored within JISNB), and therefore, will not
be included in data migration.
Financial transactions (e.g., incoming payments: fines, filing fees, bail deposits, etc., and outgoing
payments: refunds, payments to witnesses, etc.) across all three levels of court are recorded in
JISNB. Payments are currently accepted in person (via cash, debit, credit card, certified cheque,
and money order), or over the phone (via credit card). Refer to Current Interfaces – Interface 5:
Financial Information System below for additional information.
JISNB was implemented in 1982 and was upgraded to VB6 in the early 2000s.
Antiquated industry best practices have introduced challenges in the form of maintainability and
adaptability. As a result, business changes are costly and time consuming to implement, and the
Appendix E – Overview of the Department of Justice and Public Safety
antiquated programming language has resulted in challenges identifying resources to work on the
system.
In addition to the technical challenges JISNB has many business challenges which include:
• Inability to efficiently adapt to changing business requirements has resulted in significant
technical debt due to the resources required to keep JISNB operational, the length of time
required to implement updates, and competing priorities.
• Limited business rules and error proofing mechanisms allow users to make mistakes with
potentially significant impacts.
• Data not accurately captured. For example, drop-down lists not tailored to the business
requirements, or fields not large enough to accommodate the required data.
• Manual processes and document preparation can lead to inconsistencies, data entry errors,
and creates a steep learning curve. This increases staff frustration and is an inefficient use of
staff time.
• Inefficient scheduling requiring duplicate data entry between JISNB and Microsoft Outlook
calendars can result in court delays if both systems are not updated correctly. It also requires
the manual compilation of court delay statistics leading to inconsistent reporting.
• Limited flexibility to establish internal controls for monitoring and managing access, built in
controls such as edit check, process controls, and audit logs.
• Accessing data for new reporting requirements requires IT intervention.
• The absence of automated reminders, document routing, and task management can lead to
delays in court proceedings, missed deadlines, and bottlenecks in case handling.
• Lack of basic functionality available in modern case management systems. For example,
updating multiple files at the same time, or advanced searching.
NOTA:
Implemented in 2010 and built on SQL server-based data infrastructure, NOTA is used by the Court of
King’s Bench for criminal and civil law cases. NOTA in its current state is technically stable;
however, it lacks functionality to effectively capture the business requirements and digitally
transform the Court of King’s Bench.
NOTA is comprised of three-hundred and ninety-seven (397) tables across two (2) databases as
follows:
Database # Tables
Case Data 155
Code Values 242
Documents entered into NOTA are stored on a Storage Area Network (SAN), not within the
database. The current practice is to enter final orders and select briefs into NOTA, other court
documents are retained in paper format.
Challenges with NOTA include:
• Limited functionality to capture file requirements, such as full names or aliases used by an
individual.

• Scheduling for multi-day appearances needs to be entered (and updated) individually for each
day resulting in an inefficient use of staff time and the potential for data entry errors.
• Duplicate data entry is required between JISNB and NOTA when criminal law files transfer to
the Court of King’s Bench from Provincial Court.
• Limited business rules/error proofing mechanisms, and reporting functionality.
• Lack of document generation functionality.
• Accessing data for new reporting requirements requires IT intervention.
• Limited flexibility to establish internal controls for monitoring and managing access, built in
controls such as edit check, process controls, and audit logs.
• The absence of automated reminders, document routing, and task management can lead to
delays in court proceedings, missed deadlines, and bottlenecks in case handling.
• Lack of basic functionality available in modern case management systems, such as updating
multiple files at the same time, electronic filing, or advanced search functionality.
Court of Appeal case management:
Implemented in 2010 the Court of Appeal case management solution is comprised of a Microsoft
Access database and a Microsoft Outlook calendar. This presents a wide range of significant
challenges and impacts due to the limitations of these tools when applied to the complex,
sensitive, and highly regulated environment of a judicial system. The absence of automated
reminders, document routing, and task management can lead to delays in court proceedings,
missed deadlines, and bottlenecks in case handling. Court personnel spend excessive time on
administrative tasks that could be automated, leading to inefficiencies.
Some documents are stored on a shared drive; however, the paper file is the official record.
Court Stenographer Activity Reporting (CSAR):
Implemented in 2005 and built on SQL server-based data infrastructure, CSAR is used for tracking
stenographer time in court, transcript requests, and transcript invoices across all three levels of
court. While it looks like a dated system, CSAR is technically stable as the programming language
has been upgraded and it was migrated to new servers in 2024.
Documents are not stored in CSAR, and the database includes 13 tables.
Data currently tracked in CSAR will be captured in the new system moving forward; however, data
migration from CSAR is not anticipated. If after discussions with the successful Proponent, data
migration is deemed beneficial, data migration may be invoiced separately as an optional service
at the Department’s discretion. Pricing proposals should not include data migration from this
system.
Challenges with CSAR include:
• Limited data availability to accurately reflect the business requirements.
• A lack of user-friendliness.
• Reliance on manual processes for time entry calculations.

These challenges result in an inefficient use of staff time; data entry errors; and the potential for
inaccurate data for evidence-informed decision making.

Organizational Challenges
Modernizing the courts business processes and the technology that supports it is the ultimate goal of the
Department. Organizational challenges include:
1. The Courts as described above are a separate branch of government and are independent from
the Government of New Brunswick. The Court Services Branch is contained with the Government
of New Brunswick’s Department of Justice and Public Safety and provides comprehensive
administrative and operational support to all three levels of court. Information technology
services are provided to the Courts and the Court Services branch through the Government of
New Brunswick’s Department of Service New Brunswick, Technology Services.
2. This project is much more than upgrading software; it is a business transformation of the Courts
from paper-based files and processes to digital files and processes and will result in significant
change for the Courts, court users and court administration. As a result, the Courts not only want
a system that will support this vision, but also a partner who has demonstrated their ability to
transition a court to a digital environment. The Department is willing to consider business process
changes to adapt to the new software.
3. Manual processes, duplicate data entry between systems, and limited document generation
functionality can lead to inconsistencies, data entry errors, and creates a steep learning curve.
This increases staff frustration and is an inefficient use of staff time.

4. Each of the four systems in use has their own client repository/identification making it difficult to
track a client across the three levels of court. The Department would like to implement a central
client repository.

Security safeguards
The vendor will have implemented an information security management program that
includes:
• physical, technological, and administrative safeguards to protect GNB
Information from
o theft or unauthorized access leading to damage such as
o unauthorized access, copying, modification, disclosure, and disposal
o while at information is at rest, in process and in transit.
Appendix F – GNB IT Security and Procurement
• The proposed system will contain cyber security controls that meet GNB
security policies, including but not limited to
o Government Information Technology Systems Policy (GISSP)
o GNB Cloud Services Policy (where applicable)
GNB Security Policy documents can be made available by request, and under the
protection of Non-disclosure Agreements (NDA’s)
1. The GNB Cyber Security program is aligned with NIST 800-53(R5). These controls include
physical, technological, and administrative safeguards to protect GNB information.
2. The vendor’s information security management program should include the following,
at a minimum.
a. Written information security policy and procedures.
b. Defined responsibility for lifecycle management ensuring that the security
controls remain effective and adequate for the protection of GNB information.
c. An inventory and data classification structure of the facilities, systems, and
digital assets, that the vendor uses to access, use, temporarily hold, transfer GNB
information
d. Identify Authorized Personnel responsible for the operation of these
environments and digital assets and the protection of GNB information.
e. Controls to ensure that Authorized Personnel are subject to appropriate
background checks and educated and trained on the vendor’s security policies
and practices prior to being given access to GNB Information and that their
access is role-based.
f. Physical and environmental security for facilities used to process GNB
information include controls to protect from fire, flood, and other forms of
disasters.
g. Operating procedures and controls for the secure operation of systems and
networks facilitating access to GNB information reasonably prevents and limits,
should it occur, accidental or deliberate misuse, including but not be limited to
change management, least privileges granted, segregation of duties, separation
of production environment from development and test environments, backups,
network security, the encryption of GNB Information, and secure mechanisms
for accessing GNB information. The preferred mechanism for accessing GNB
information is using one of GNB’s approved Remote Access solutions.
h. Access controls and procedures for the authorization, regular review, and
revocation of Authorized Personnel access are reviewed to reasonably ensure
that their access to GNB information is appropriate for their role and effective,
regardless of their location and the tools they use to gain access.
i. Policies, processes and controls to ensure timely recognition, containment,
escalation, investigation and reporting to the Custodians of suspected and actual
security breaches, monitoring of compliance with such policies and procedures,
and measures to mitigate any resulting harm.
Appendix F – GNB IT Security and Procurement
j. Processes and controls, that meet industry standards, to ensure the secure
destruction, disposition or sanitization of media containing of GNB information.
k. A solution to manage security information logs and retention of such logs for a
rolling one (1) year, that aligns with GNB Security Operation Center procedures.
l. Regular control reviews of the security of the Services, including, as applicable,
penetration testing. An attestation that includes, at a minimum, the date, time
and type of assessment performed and the vendor’s commitment to address any
threats or vulnerabilities identified.
3. The following are cyber security controls that are considered a priority, for
Services/Solutions that process and store GNB Information.
a. Integration with GNB Authentication and Authorization systems
b. Multi Factor Authentication
c. Integration of system event logging with GNB Security Operation Center
processes and tools
d. Lifecycle management of patches and vulnerabilities
e. Agreement on escalation process for Cybersecurity related incidents

ii. SOC 2 Type II (cloud-based systems)

APPENDIX G – PRIVACY PROTECTION REQUIREMENTS
Definitions
“Act” means the Right to Information and Protection of Privacy Act, S.N.B. 2009, c. R-10.6, or
other applicable Acts.
“Privacy Breach” means any incident of unauthorized access, use, disclosure or disposal of
personal information in the custody of or under the control of the Province.
“Ombud” means the New Brunswick Ombud, the Privacy Commissioner of Canada and/or
another province or territory’s legislated privacy oversight body.
“Contract’ means a contract between the Province and a Contractor.
“Contractor” means any person or company that undertakes a contract with the Province to
provide materials or labour to perform a service or do a job which involves the creation or
collection of or access to personal information, and includes any subcontractor or agent
retained by the Contractor to perform its obligations under the contract with the Province.
“Personal Information” means recorded information about an identifiable individual. It includes
information that identifies the individual or for which it is reasonably foreseeable in the
circumstances that it could be utilized, either alone or with other information, to identify the
individual.
“Province” means the Government of New Brunswick as represented by Service NB.
“Security Arrangements” means any administrative, technical and/or physical safeguards to
protect against a breach of information security.
Purpose
1. The purpose of this Schedule is to identify privacy protection requirements that will apply
to a Contractor to:
1. enable the Province to comply with its statutory obligations under the Act with
respect to personal information; and
2. ensure that, as a service provider, a Contractor is aware of and complies with
these statutory obligations.
Ownership and Control
2. Any personal information provided to a Contractor by the Province, or created or
collected by a Contractor as an agent of the Province pursuant to a Contract (hereinafter
collectively referred to as “Personal Information”), is under the control of the Province
and unless otherwise expressly agreed to in writing by the Province remains the sole
property of the Province and must be returned to the Province at the end of the Contract
as instructed by the Province.
Appendix G – Privacy Protection Requirements
3. Personal Information provided to a Contractor by the Province under 2. is strictly to fulfil
the purposes of the Contract and is provided under a relationship of utmost confidence
and trust.
4. The collection, use, disclosure, security, storage and disposal of Personal Information
and all other information exchanged between a Contractor and the Province pursuant to
a Contract is subject to the Act and other laws applicable to the Province.
5. The Contractor acknowledges that the Province is a ‘public body’ under the Act and that
unless otherwise provided in the Act the Province must grant access to information in its
custody or under its control when requested by any person pursuant to the Act. The
Contractor agrees to treat as confidential information all requests it receives pursuant to
the Act or otherwise for information created, collected, used or disclosed for purposes of
fulfilling its obligations under the Contract.
Collection of Personal Information
6. Unless otherwise specified in a Contract with the Province or directed in writing by the
Province, a Contractor must:
1. only collect or create the minimum amount of Personal Information necessary for
the performance of the Contractor’s obligations, or the exercise of the
Contractor’s rights, under a Contract the Province;
2. collect Personal Information directly from the individual the information is about;
and
3. inform an individual from whom it collects Personal Information of the purpose
and legal authority for collecting the information, and the title, business address
and telephone number of an officer or employee who can answer the individual’s
questions about the collection.
Access to Personal Information
7. A Contractor must identify and designate all Contractor employees who will have access
to Personal Information, or identify positions of employees who will have access. It must
also maintain some form of audit trail (electronic or paper form) to demonstrate that
those who accessed Personal Information had the proper authority to do so.
Use or Disclosure of Personal Information
8. A Contractor must not use or disclose Personal Information for any purpose other than
the performance of its obligations in the applicable Contract or to comply with the law.
Protection of Personal Information
9. A Contractor must make and maintain reasonable physical, organizational and
technological safeguards to ensure the confidentiality, accuracy, integrity and
completeness of Personal Information and to protect the Personal Information against
any loss or theft and unauthorized access, use, disclosure, destruction or copying. This
includes security arrangements specified by the Province in the Contract.
Right of Access and Correction of Personal Information
10. If a Contractor receives a request for access to or correction of Personal Information
from a person other than the Province, the Contractor:
Appendix G – Privacy Protection Requirements
1. must promptly advise the person to make the request to the Province, and
2. must not disclose or attempt to correct the Personal Information in response to
such requests unless otherwise expressly instructed in writing by the Province.
11. A Contractor must assist the Province in responding to requests for access to or
correction of Personal Information as instructed by the Province and at no cost to
Province.
Storage
12. A Contractor must not store Personal Information outside Canada or permit access to
Personal Information from outside Canada unless instructed to do so in writing by the
Province.
Retention of Personal Information
13. Unless a Contract otherwise specifies, a Contractor must retain Personal Information as
instructed in writing by the Province until the Province requests its return or destruction.
Reproduction, Return or Destruction of Personal Information
14. At any time upon the written direction of the Province, a Contractor must immediately
return all Personal Information to the Province and/or destroy any and all Personal
Information. A Contractor must not retain any copies or other reproductions thereof. All

readable and usable by the Province. Furthermore, a Contractor must, upon request by
the Province, provide written confirmation to the Province that the terms and conditions
of this section have been complied with.

Privacy Breach

Executive Summary
The Province of New Brunswick is seeking a fully bilingual, cloud-based Court Case Management System to replace
four legacy systems and unify digital operations across all three levels of court. The solution must be highly
configurable, with minimal to no customization, and deliver out-of-the-box capabilities such as electronic filing, digital
case files, public and partner portals, automated workflows, judicial tools, scheduling, financial management, and
document generation. It must integrate with multiple systems, meet all security, privacy, and data-residency
requirements, and support a low-risk, phased implementation model with strong change-management and long-term
operational support. CGI’s proposed solution has been developed explicitly to meet these expectations.
CGI is proudly Canadian, founded and headquartered in Canada, and has delivered services across Atlantic
Canada for more than 40 of its nearly 50 years in operation. As a long-time community builder, we reinvest in local
talent and support the economic and digital evolution of New Brunswick. Supported by nearly 100,000
professionals worldwide, CGI brings both local accountability and global expertise, aligning seamlessly with the
Province’s long-term vision for justice modernization.
CGI’s proposed solution is designed to support New Brunswick’s transition from paper-based processes to a modern,
digital justice environment. CGI’s most significant differentiator is that our approach is grounded in real, proven
experience delivering Canada’s largest multi-court modernization through the Lexius program in Quebec, experience
that distinguishes us in the Canadian justice sector. We bring a bilingual team with deep justice-sector expertise, a
strong local presence, and continuity across government modernization programs. Our solution is highly
configurable, not custom-built, ensuring long-term sustainability, lower costs, and seamless future upgrades aligned
with Microsoft’s platform evolution.
Our system provides a unified digital platform across all three levels of court, offering e-filing, digital case files, partner
portals, automated workflows, and support for virtual and hybrid hearings. A proven integration framework ensures
full alignment with New Brunswick’s interoperability requirements. The solution reduces administrative burden,
improves service delivery, and supports fully bilingual operations across user interfaces, workflows, templates,
notifications, and reporting.
CGI’s delivery approach emphasizes stability and predictability through a structured, phased implementation that
minimizes disruption and ensures each court is fully prepared for go-live. Training, readiness assessments, and
robust user support help staff and judiciary adapt smoothly to new workflows. Our methodology aligns directly with
the Province’s preferred phased approach, featuring clear governance checkpoints and measurable user readiness,
reflecting lessons learned from real-world Canadian justice programs.
Security, privacy, and data residency are foundational to our solution. All information is hosted exclusively in Canada,
and our architecture fully complies with the Province’s strict data-residency rules, ensuring all data, including
metadata, remains 100% within Canada at rest and in transit. The solution meets all mandatory technical and Cloud
Policy requirements, and CGI actively supports the Province’s governance processes, including PIA, TRA, BIA, and
executive approvals.
CGI also provides a comprehensive operational support model for the full term of the agreement, including help desk
services, SLA management, monitoring, performance management, continuity planning, and disaster recovery,
ensuring long-term stability post-go-live. CGI’s proposed solution fully meets New Brunswick’s requirement for a
configurable, SaaS-based CMS with no customization, relying entirely on out-of-the-box functionality to ensure
maintainability, upgradeability, and long-term sustainability. The platform’s low-code, configuration-based design also
enables New Brunswick to adopt future Microsoft innovations, including analytics and AI enhancements, without
redevelopment.

1.3000000000000003,AI Model Architecture and Parameters,"Proposals should provide detail on the AI model architecture and the different parameters available to ""tune"" the model to satisfy the different use-cases; trade-off due to the change in parameters; and their impacts on the model and the biases.",H,"The proposed system uses AI capabilities built on Microsoft Azure AI and Azure OpenAI Service. These models operate within the Dynamics 365 and Power Platform environment and are supported by Azure Machine Learning for tuning, evaluation and responsible operation. The AI architecture supports supervised, unsupervised and generative learning using Azure OpenAI models and Azure ML-managed configuration.
AI Model Architecture

AI capabilities in the system use Azure OpenAI models including GPT-4o, GPT-4o mini, GPT-4.1, o-series models and embedding models. These models are accessed securely through Azure OpenAI Service and integrated with Dynamics 365 via Dataverse. For scenarios requiring custom tuning or training, Azure Machine Learning provides an architecture that supports parameterized experiments, hyperparameter sweeps, controlled search spaces and automated optimization workflows.
Tunable Parameters
Azure Machine Learning supports tuning through the SweepJob framework, allowing administrators and data scientists to configure:
• Hyperparameter search spaces, including discrete values (Choice), continuous values (Uniform, Normal, LogUniform, LogNormal) and advanced distributions such as QNormal and QLogUniform
• Sampling algorithms, including random sampling, grid sampling and Bayesian optimization
• Primary metric selection and optimization goal (Maximize or Minimize)
• Early termination policies, including Bandit Policy, Median Stopping Policy and Truncation Selection Policy
• Resource limits such as max_total_trials, max_concurrent_trials, timeout and trial_timeout

Example tunable parameters include learning_rate, number_of_hidden_layers, batch_size, dropout_rate and keep_probability. For generative models, tunable parameters include temperature, max_tokens and top_p.
Trade-offs Associated With Parameter Tuning
Adjustments to hyperparameters can affect model performance, cost, stability and fairness. Examples include:
• Increasing learning_rate can accelerate convergence while reducing stability
• Increasing model complexity or number_of_hidden_layers may improve accuracy while increasing overfitting risk
• Higher dropout_rate supports generalization but may reduce accuracy
• Higher temperature or top_p increases creativity in generative models while reducing predictability and increasing hallucination risk
• Expanding the search space or increasing trial count improves model selection quality but increases compute cost and experiment duration
Azure Machine Learning provides visualization tools such as metrics charts, parallel coordinates charts and scatter plots to help teams evaluate and compare these trade-offs.
Impact on Bias and Mitigation Tools

Changes to hyperparameters can amplify or reduce bias depending on their effect on error distribution across data subgroups. Azure Machine Learning supports responsible AI practices and provides tools for fairness assessment, error analysis, interpretability and counterfactual testing. These tools help identify:
• Differences in model performance across sensitive groups
• Cohorts with high error concentration
• Local and global feature importance
• Scenarios where outputs may be unreliable or inconsistent

Mitigation approaches include dataset balancing, adjusting hyperparameter ranges, selecting alternative sampling strategies and applying interpretation-driven tuning. Azure Machine Learning can generate Responsible AI scorecards to document fairness, transparency and safety considerations for governance and audit purposes.
Summary

Dynamics 365 AI features are powered by Azure’s model architecture and can be tuned using Azure Machine Learning tools. Administrators and data scientists can configure hyperparameters, search strategies and optimization criteria, and evaluate tuning decisions using built-in fairness, error analysis and interpretability tools. This ensures high-quality AI outcomes that align with performance, governance and fairness requirements."

1.5000000000000004,AI Data Anonymization and De-identification,Proposals should provide a detailed description of the AI data anonymization and de-identification processes.,H,"The proposed system provides comprehensive data anonymization and de-identification capabilities using the combined features of Dynamics 365, the Microsoft Power Platform, Microsoft Purview, and Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps. 1.6000000000000005,AI Data Isolation,"Proposals should describe how data isolation is guaranteed in accordance to the GNB Privacy and Security policies regarding data, and what measures are in place to avoid data-leakage.",H,"1. Guaranteeing Data Isolation

1. INTRODUCTION / BACKGROUND
Service New Brunswick's (SNB) Customer eXperience Management (CXM) Program provides a strategic approach to
delivering case management solutions across the Government of New Brunswick (GNB). Through two competitive
processes – one to select enterprise platforms and another to identify qualified implementation partners – four (4)
platforms were selected (Microsoft Dynamics, Salesforce, Oracle CX and Qualtrics) along with a network of
implementation partners. The CXM Program ensures case management solutions are built on the right platform,
using an iterative, client-centric approach, and supported using a common operational model.
The purpose of this Statement of Work (SOW) is to establish a collaborative engagement with a Vendor who will
serve as a delivery partner to support the successful implementation of a series of customer experience (CXM)
initiatives on the Salesforce platform. These initiatives are aligned with our organization’s broader CXM program
goals to modernize service delivery, improve digital access, and streamline interactions with clients and partners.
The selected Vendor will become a key contributor within a cross-functional DevOps team that operates under a
scaled Agile delivery model. This Vendor and SNB will be responsible for the iterative delivery of solutions across
multiple projects over the course of the engagement. The Vendor is expected to bring the necessary roles and
expertise to complement internal SNB resources and collaborate closely with internal stakeholders and governance
bodies.
The engagement will focus on continuous value delivery through well-established Agile practices, active backlog
management, and alignment with CXM program standards and oversight.
Only Vendors who have been pre-qualified on Tender #8023113-23 Customer Experience Management (CXM)
Implementation Partners for Salesforce are eligible to respond to this Statement of Work (SOW).
2. SERVICES SOUGHT
SNB is seeking to engage an Implementation Partner for the provision of a scalable team of Salesforce IT professionals
for a period of three (3) years and within an estimated total budget of $10 million. The selected Vendor will
collaborate closely with SNB’s internal teams to design and implement targeted IT solutions that address specific
business challenges throughout the contract term. This engagement is intended to enhance SNB’s existing capabilities
by integrating Vendor resources into the current environment, leveraging their specialized expertise, adaptability, and
additional capacity to accelerate solution delivery and drive measurable business outcomes. This opportunity is non-
exclusive and does not preclude SNB from acquiring services from other partners or vendors for similar or
complementary services.
The specific roles and number of Vendor resources required will vary over the course of the engagement, depending
on the size, complexity, and phase of each project. Resource needs will fluctuate as projects ramp up and/or ramp
down, transition into support, or as new initiatives are onboarded. The Vendor must be able to adapt to these
changes and scale their team(s) accordingly, ensuring appropriate coverage for both delivery and sustainment

5. ALIGNMENT WITH CXM PROGRAM
The Customer eXperience Management (CXM) Program is a strategic initiative focused on delivering consistent,
seamless, and user-centered digital services to citizens. The program is designed to ensure that all citizen-facing
solutions across Departments are built on scalable, maintainable, and reusable architecture, with a strong emphasis
on maximizing Salesforce platform value. By establishing clear standards, reusable components, governance
processes, and a centralized CXM Gateway (see below), the program helps ensure that digital solutions are aligned
with enterprise strategies, compliant with security, privacy and integration requirements, and adaptable for long-
term evolution.
The CXM Program provides governance, architectural oversight, and shared assets/artifacts to accelerate project
delivery, reduce duplication, and promote alignment across government services. Vendors delivering solutions under
the CXM Program are expected to work within this established framework and contribute to the overall coherence
and quality of the CXM ecosystem. Furthermore, Vendors must commit to, and demonstrate alignment with, delivery
using industry standard DevOps and Scaled Agile Framework (SAFe) principles. CXM Program guidance covers delivery
methodology, architecture, design patterns, data modeling, integration, security, and user experience. Central to this
is the CXM Gateway, a curated knowledge base where Vendors can access all current CXM standards, frameworks,
templates, and approval workflows to guide compliant solution delivery.

retrospectives.

rollback strategies.

“personal information” means recorded information about an identifiable individual. It includes information that

KPI: Average number of story points completed per sprint over time.

KPI: Number of defects found per sprint, categorized by severity (critical, high, medium, low).

Issue Response and Resolution Timelines

Build/Deployment Success Rate
KPI: % of successful builds and deployments without rollback (target ≥ 95%).
Why it matters: Reflects maturity of DevOps automation and stability of environments.
CGI Practice: Automated CI/CD pipelines (ADO + Copado) enforce gated deployments with rollback plans.

KPI: % of artifacts submitted to CXM Gateway on time, relative to sprint/PI milestones (target 100%).

collection of or access to personal information, and includes any subcontractor or agent
retained by the Contractor to perform its obligations under the contract with the Province.
“personal information” means recorded information about an identifiable individual. It includes
information that identifies the individual or for which it is reasonably foreseeable in the
circumstances that it could be utilized, either alone or with other information, to identify the
individual.

protect against a breach of information security.

respect to personal information; and

To whom it may concern,
On behalf of CGI, I would like to thank you for giving us the opportunity to submit this proposal in response to your Request for Proposal for Tender #8026125-26 Managed Detection & Response.

CGI is a Canadian multinational information technology consulting and systems integration company, established 49 years ago in Quebec City in 1976 by our two founders, Serge Godin, our current Chairman of the Board, and André Imbeau, former board member and advisor to the Chairman. Since opening our first Atlantic Canada office in 1991, CGI has expanded its services and presence, employing ~800 professionals across Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, and Newfoundland. Our service mix now includes systems integration, IT consulting, business process services, and software application management, supported by local consulting practices, a global delivery center, and extensive infrastructure services. In 2001, CGI reinforced its commitment to Atlantic Canada through a landmark agreement with Service New Brunswick Inc., establishing our “g-Commerce Lab” at Fredericton’s Knowledge Park, which continues to drive innovation and government service delivery worldwide. Today, CGI is one of Atlantic Canada’s largest IT employers, delivering a full breadth of services to clients across Canada, the U.S., and around the globe.

CGI's Pricing Methodology Overview

CGI typically employs a "fixed fee" pricing model with measurable KPIs for MDR services, providing clients with price predictability for budgeting while maintaining control over support costs. Unlike traditional rigid fixed fee models, CGI offers a transparent "effort-based" fee model derived from baseline KPIs such as number of incidents, requests, changes, etc.

As part of the pricing methodology, CGI conducts a Current Situation Assessment (CSA) during knowledge transfer and onboarding to collaboratively confirm detailed contact volumes. Variables considered for pricing typically include coverage hours, asset volume, and response time SLA, to name a few. The operational delivery structure utilizes a shared service model, though dedicated models are optionally available

The pricing approach includes a monthly baseline volume supplemented by a price "per additional volume" over baseline. Through mutually agreed upon governance processes, CGI works with clients to understand and manage these volumes, finding opportunities for efficiencies, savings, and improved service performance.  CGI actively reviews changes in service demands that may require right-sizing and re-alignment based on current or future requirements.
Additional pricing methodologies, including pure-volumetric, bank of hours, Time and Materials (T&M), etc. are also available depending on the services and scope involved.

6.0 BACKGROUND INFORMATION
6.1 GENERAL OVERVIEW OF SERVICE NEW BRUNSWICK:
The Government of New Brunswick (GNB), in the interest of reducing costs
through duplication of services, has consolidated into a shared services
organization that encompasses many common government services, including
information systems. As part of this consolidation, one of the goals for IT
Services is to seek efficiencies through the consolidation and centralization of its
technology solutions and infrastructure.
One of the key areas of responsibility for Service New Brunswick is Technology
Services, which includes the management and operations of the Government of
New Brunswick’s (GNB) Data Centres.
With the solution resulting from this RFP, Service New Brunswick Technology
Services seeks to implement a data centre infrastructure management (DCIM)
solution using a centralized management model.
Service New Brunswick (SNB) currently administers, on behalf of the
Government of New Brunswick (GNB), the procurement and operation of 13 data
centres of various capacities located in New Brunswick. Data centre technologies
and related services for Parts 1, 2 and 3 of GNB including but not limited to:
• Housing of physical devices
o Cabinets
o Power Distribution Units (PDU)
o Structured data cabling
• Provide redundant power to all devices
• Backup power stream
o Uninterruptable Power Supply(s) (UPS)
o Automatic power Transfer Switch(s) (ATS)
o Generator(s)
• Physical Security of all data centre devices and facilities
6.2 SERVICES REQUIRED BY SERVICE NEW BRUNSWICK:
Overview
Service New Brunswick (SNB) is seeking proposals from qualified vendors to
provide a comprehensive SaaS DCIM solution. This solution must enable full life-
cycle asset management, power and network monitoring, capacity planning, and
integration with third-party systems.
1. Core Requirements
Asset Management
The DCIM solution must:
• Provide life-cycle management for designing, deploying, and
decommissioning assets.
• Track and manage data center components, including:
• Environmental probes
• Power systems
• Network equipment
• Cabinets
• Support:
• Over 40 predefined data fields with unlimited customization.
• Visualization of asset placement and movement between locations.
• Bulk updates for data and power port configurations.
• Offer advanced search, filter capabilities, and customizable dashboards.
Data Visualization
The solution must:
• Provide accurate equipment modeling with multiple layered floor plans.
• Support full cabling infrastructure management, including:
• Real-time visualizations of circuit building and structured cabling.
• Capacity metrics for cable paths and tray design visualization.
2. Power Chain Management
The DCIM solution must fully model the entire power chain, including:
• Utility providers, UPS systems, PDU outlets, and other components.
• 3-phase power monitoring, circuit breakers, and fuses.
• Redundancy and dependency analysis for UPS banks and power chains.
• Custom configurations for power socket types, standard connectors, and
labels.
3. Capacity Planning
The solution must offer:
• Visibility into power, network, cooling, and space resources.
• Resource forecasting and conflict detection for installations, moves, adds,
or changes.
• Automatic adjustments of planned vs. current resource states.
• Support for customizable workflows and detailed work orders with
instructions.
4. Monitoring Tools
Facilities Monitoring
The solution must:
• Provide a unified interface for real-time alarm management across
locations.
• Track metrics such as:
• Power efficiency (PUE/DCIE) and energy consumption.
• Environmental changes (temperature, humidity, airflow).
• Offer Branch Circuit Monitoring and historical data storage.
Visualization and Alerts
• Provide customizable thresholds for alerts and notifications.
• Support advanced visualization with user-supplied diagrams and event
playback.
5. Integration and Security
APIs and Compatibility
The solution must include:
• Open, fee-free Restful APIs for seamless module integration.
• Compatibility with third-party ITSM systems and industry-standard
devices.
Authentication and Deployment
• Granular, role-based permissions with integration options like:
• Active Directory (AD), LDAP, or SAML 2.0.
• Deployable as a virtual appliance with features such as:
• Built-in high availability and automated backups.
• Regular software and security updates.
6. Licensing and Support
Licensing Model
Vendors must provide:
• A subscription-based model covering all features without restrictions on
users, devices, or locations.
• Licensing based on cabinets and devices, with no modular add-on
charges.
Technical Support
The vendor must:
• Provide enterprise-class product support with a minimum of 8x5 coverage
and 10 monthly support hours. Preference will be given to proponents
that are able to offer support coverage M-F 9am-5pm AST.
• Offer escalation paths and service level agreements (SLAs) to prioritize
issues.
7. Term
The award of this RFP will result in the negotiation of a Contract of Supply with
the successful vendor. Upon the successful completion of negotiations, a
Contract of Supply will be established for a period of three (3) years, with the
option to renew for seven (7) optional years beyond the end of the initial term,
renewed annually or in multiple-years, as negotiated and agreed upon by both
parties.

7.3 PRICING
As part of the response to Section 7.3, proponents must submit a detailed Price
Schedule in Appendix D – Pricing Proposals. The pricing submission must align
with the data provided in Section 6.3, Table 1, and shall clearly outline all
associated costs for the proposed solution.
To ensure a fair and consistent evaluation of pricing across varying deployment
models, proposals will be assessed based on the total cost of ownership
(TCO) over a period of thirty-six (36) months. This evaluation will consider both
direct and indirect costs, as specified below:
Pricing Requirements:
• Firm Pricing: All pricing must remain firm for at least the initial three (3)
years of the contract term.
• Currency: All prices must be quoted in Canadian dollars (CAD) and must
exclude applicable taxes.
• Comprehensive Costs: Proponents must clearly identify and itemize all
costs associated with their proposed solutions, including licensing,
support, maintenance, implementation, cloud hosting, and any additional
fees or required services.
• Potential price increases for the optional renewal years will be limited to
2% per year or the New Brunswick Consumer Price Index (NB CPI) for the

8.0 EVALUATION PROCEDURE

The process will include a review and check of the information contained in the

2 General Requirements
CGI, in partnership with Nlyte, proposes the implementation of a commercially proven Data Center Infrastructure Management
(DCIM) platform designed to deliver centralized visibility, governance, and operational control across data center, colocation,
and distributed edge environments.
The proposed solution provides a comprehensive system of record for both physical and virtual infrastructure assets. Through
advanced visualization, structured operational workflows, and robust reporting capabilities, the platform enables informed
decision-making, strengthens governance, and improves overall operational efficiency.
2.1 Capabilities and Scope
Core Functional Capabilities
The DCIM platform delivers a fully integrated set of capabilities that support infrastructure lifecycle management, operational
oversight, and enterprise alignment. The solution provides:
• Asset and Infrastructure Modeling
The solution provides detailed modeling of racks, cabinets, power chains, and connectivity relationships, establishing
a centralized and authoritative infrastructure system of record.
• Power and Capacity Management
Comprehensive monitoring and reporting of power utilization, space availability, and infrastructure capacity support
proactive planning, risk mitigation, and optimized resource utilization.
• Workflow and Change Governance
Structured Install, Move, Add, and Change (IMAC) workflows introduce formal change governance, reducing
operational risk and ensuring accountability across infrastructure modifications.
• Visualization and Reporting
Multi-level visualizations across rooms, areas, cages, and sites provide clear operational insight. Configurable
dashboards and exportable reports support both day-to-day management and executive oversight.
• Enterprise Integration
Native APIs and prebuilt connectors enable integration with ITSM platforms, CMDBs, virtualization tools, and other
enterprise systems, ensuring alignment with existing processes and systems of record.
• Role-Based Access Control
Secure, web-based access with enterprise directory integration ensures appropriate data access and governance
across stakeholder groups.
Architectural Overview
The solution is web-based and configuration-driven, minimizing the need for custom development while simplifying future
upgrades and maintenance. Its scalable architecture supports centralized management of multiple locations, with logical
segmentation by site, tenant, or organizational structure.
Designed for enterprise environments, the platform integrates seamlessly within the existing technology ecosystem without
disrupting established systems of record.
Scope Clarification
The proposed solution is a Data Center Infrastructure Management (DCIM) platform and is distinct from a Building
Management System (BMS).
While both systems operate within the data center environment, their purposes differ:
• DCIM provides infrastructure visibility, asset management, power monitoring, and operational governance.
© 2026 CGI Inc. Confidential 2
